han.name: Han court
han.note: Deliberately the palest thing on the map -- near-neutral, so the warlords read as colour against it. The imperial government as an independent actor: whoever holds the Emperor. Shrinks to nothing after Cao Cao takes him to Xuchang in ch. 14.

shu.name: Shu Han
shu.note: Liu Bei's following, from two men in a Zhuo county garden to the western empire.

wei.name: Cao Wei
wei.note: Cao Cao's power, later the Wei dynasty.

wu.name: Eastern Wu
wu.note: The Sun family's south-east, from Sun Jian through Sun Ce to Sun Quan.

jin.name: Jin
jin.note: The Sima family's dynasty, proclaimed in ch. 119. Sima Yi, Shi and Zhao stay Wei-coloured: they served Wei for their whole careers, and the novel treats them as Wei's commanders.

yellowturban.name: Yellow Turbans
yellowturban.note: Zhang Jue's rising. Territory here means districts in revolt, not administration.

lijueguosi.name: Li Jue and Guo Si
lijueguosi.note: Dong Zhuo's officers, who inherit Chang'an and the Emperor after ch. 9.

taoqian.name: Tao Qian
taoqian.note: Xuzhou, willed to Liu Bei in ch. 12.

liubiao.name: Liu Biao
liubiao.note: Jing province, the buffer Liu Bei shelters in for seven years.

liuzhang.name: Liu Zhang
liuzhang.note: Yi province, inherited from his father Liu Yan. Absorbed by Liu Bei in ch. 65.

xiliang.name: Ma Teng and Han Sui
xiliang.note: The Liang province horsemen of the north-west.

zhanglu.name: Zhang Lu
zhanglu.note: The Five Pecks of Rice theocracy in Hanzhong.

nanman.name: Nanman
nanman.note: Meng Huo's southern tribes, campaigned against in ch. 87-90.

unaligned.name: Unaligned
unaligned.note: Fallback for figures with no standing allegiance.

liubei.note: A mat-weaver claiming descent from Prince Jing of Zhongshan. The novel's moral centre and its most restless traveller.

guanyu.note: Later deified as the god of war.

zhaoyun.note: First met in ch. 7 fighting for Gongsun Zan; does not join Liu Bei for good until ch. 28.

zhugeliang.note: 諸葛 is read Gia Cát in Vietnamese, not the regular Chư Cát.

liushan.role: Second and last emperor of Shu

caocao.role: Chancellor of Han; founder of Wei
caocao.note: Judged in the novel as 'a capable minister in a peaceful age, a treacherous hero in a chaotic one'.

xiahoudun.note: Swallows his own eye at Xiapi, ch. 18.

dianwei.note: Dies covering Cao Cao's escape at Wan, ch. 16.

zhangliao.note: Lü Bu's officer until ch. 19, then Cao Cao's best field commander.

simayi.role: Wei commander; grandfather of the Jin dynasty

jiaxu.note: Serves Dong Zhuo's officers, then Zhang Xiu, then Cao Cao, and outlives them all.

sunjian.note: Finds the Imperial Seal in a well at Luoyang, ch. 6; killed attacking Liu Biao, ch. 7.

sunce.note: Conquers the south-east in ch. 15 with borrowed troops.

taishici.note: Breaks the siege of Beihai for Kong Rong in ch. 11 before ever meeting the Sun family.

huanggai.note: Takes the beating that sells the false defection at Red Cliffs, ch. 46.

ganning.note: A river pirate before he was an admiral.

lvmeng.note: Takes Jing province from Guan Yu, ch. 75.

luxun.note: Burns Liu Bei's camps at Xiaoting, ch. 84.

emperorxian.note: Enthroned by Dong Zhuo at nine years old; a hostage of one warlord or another for the rest of his life.

wangyun.note: Author of the chain stratagem that destroys Dong Zhuo.

dongcheng.note: Receives the girdle edict in ch. 20.

hejin.note: Summons Dong Zhuo to the capital and is murdered by the eunuchs before he arrives, ch. 3.

zhangjue.note: Styles himself General of Heaven. Dies of illness mid-rebellion, ch. 2.

huaxiong.note: Killed by Guan Yu before the wine cooled, ch. 5.

yuanshao.note: Head of a family with 'three dukes in four generations', and the coalition's chosen leader.

yuanshu.note: Declares himself emperor on the strength of the stolen seal, ch. 17.

lvbu.role: The finest warrior of the age
lvbu.note: 'Among men, Lü Bu; among horses, Red Hare.' Kills two adoptive fathers.

diaochan.note: Fictional. The novel's chain stratagem turns on her; the histories know only an unnamed maid of Dong Zhuo's.

chengong.note: Releases Cao Cao, rides with him, then leaves him over the murder of Lü Boshe's family, ch. 4.

gongsunzan.note: Liu Bei's schoolfellow under Lu Zhi, and his first patron.

lvboshe.note: Killed with his whole household in ch. 4, on a misheard sentence about a pig.

weiyan.note: Zhuge Liang distrusts him from the moment they meet, and leaves a plan for his death.

masu.note: Loses Jieting by camping on a hill with no water, and is executed weeping, ch. 96.

liufeng.note: Executed for failing to relieve Guan Yu, ch. 79.

yanyan.note: Released by Zhang Fei, and opens the road to Chengdu in return, ch. 63.

zhugezhan.note: Dies with his own son at Mianzhu, ch. 117.

liuchen.note: Kills his family and himself rather than see Shu surrender, ch. 118.

zhanghe.note: Killed in the ambush at Mumen, ch. 101.

pangde.note: Carries his own coffin to fight Guan Yu, ch. 74.

xuyou.note: Defects from Yuan Shao and gives Cao Cao the Wuchao granaries, ch. 30.

caozhi.note: Composes the seven-pace poem to save his life, ch. 79.

yangxiu.note: Executed for reading Cao Cao's mind once too often, ch. 72.

caoshuang.note: Destroyed by Sima Yi's feigned senility, ch. 106.

caomao.note: Killed in the street attempting a coup against Sima Zhao, ch. 114.

wenyang.note: Rides alone through Sima Shi's army, ch. 110.

chezhou.note: Killed by Guan Yu at the city gate, ch. 21.

duyu.note: Conquers Wu and reunites the empire, ch. 120.

zhangzhao.note: Leads the party for surrender before Red Cliffs.

dingfeng.note: Attacks through the snow in shirtsleeves, ch. 108.

sunshangxiang.note: Married to Liu Bei as bait for a trap that fails, ch. 54.

jiping.note: Tortured to death for trying to poison Cao Cao, ch. 23.

miheng.note: Strips naked to insult Cao Cao, and is sent to his death by proxy, ch. 23.

chenlin.note: His denunciation of Cao Cao cures Cao Cao's headache, ch. 22.

liucong.note: Surrenders Jing province without a fight, ch. 40.

caimao.note: Executed by Cao Cao on a forged letter, ch. 45.

huangzu.note: Killed Sun Jian; killed in turn by Sun Quan, ch. 38.

zhangsong.note: Offers Liu Bei the map of Shu, ch. 60.

zhangren.note: Kills Pang Tong at Fallen Phoenix Slope, ch. 63.

menghuo.note: Captured and released seven times, ch. 87-90.

zhurong.note: Claims descent from the god of fire, and fights better than her husband.

huatuo.note: Scrapes the poison from Guan Yu's bone; killed by Cao Cao for proposing to open his skull.

simahui.note: Tells Liu Bei that Sleeping Dragon or Young Phoenix would be enough, ch. 35.

yuji.note: Executed by Sun Ce, who then dies of the haunting, ch. 29.

mengda.note: Serves Liu Zhang, then Liu Bei, then Wei, then tries to return.

madai.note: Carries out Zhuge Liang's posthumous order and kills Wei Yan, ch. 105.

dengzhi.note: Rebuilds the alliance after Yiling, ch. 86.

wanglang.note: Argues with Zhuge Liang from horseback and dies of it, ch. 93.

luoyang.note: Han capital until Dong Zhuo burns it in ch. 6.

changan.note: Former Western Han capital; Dong Zhuo's refuge from ch. 6.

xuchang.note: Cao Cao's seat, and the Emperor's cage, from ch. 14.

ye.note: Yuan Shao's capital, later Cao Cao's northern seat.

chengdu.note: Capital of Yi province, then of Shu Han.

jianye.note: Sun Quan's capital; called Moling 秣陵 before 212.

zhuo.note: Liu Bei's home county. The peach garden oath, ch. 1.

yijing.note: Gongsun Zan's fortress, where he burns himself in ch. 21.

xiangping.note: Seat of the Gongsun family of Liaodong.

pingyuan.note: Liu Bei's first real post, granted by Gongsun Zan.

nanpi.note: Bohai commandery, Yuan Shao's original base.

puyang.note: Lü Bu's base while he holds Yan province, ch. 11-12.

beihai.note: Kong Rong's command; besieged in ch. 11.

xiaopei.note: The small town Liu Bei is repeatedly parked in.

wan.note: Nanyang. Zhang Xiu's seat; Dian Wei dies covering Cao Cao's retreat here in ch. 16.

shouchun.note: Yuan Shu's capital, and where he declares himself emperor in ch. 17.

hefei.note: The hinge of the Wei-Wu frontier for forty years.

danyang.note: The commandery that supplies the Sun family's best infantry.

chaisang.note: Sun Quan's forward headquarters during the Red Cliffs campaign.

xiangyang.note: Liu Biao's capital in Jing province.

fancheng.note: Across the Han from Xiangyang. Guan Yu's last campaign, ch. 73-76.

xinye.note: The border town Liu Biao lends Liu Bei as a shield against Cao Cao.

maicheng.note: Guan Yu is taken here, ch. 77.

hulao.note: Where the three brothers fight Lü Bu, ch. 5.

sishui.note: Hua Xiong's gate. Historically the same place as Hulao; the novel makes them two.

tongguan.note: Cao Cao against Ma Chao, ch. 58-59.

jieqiao.note: Yuan Shao against Gongsun Zan, ch. 7.

wuchao.note: Yuan Shao's granaries, burnt in ch. 30.

baima.note: Guan Yu kills Yan Liang, ch. 25.

hanzhong.note: Zhang Lu's theocracy, then the gate between Wei and Shu.

dingjun.note: Huang Zhong kills Xiahou Yuan, ch. 71.

jiange.note: The pass Jiang Wei holds while Deng Ai goes around it, ch. 117.

shangyong.note: Liu Feng and Meng Da fail to relieve Guan Yu from here, ch. 76.

jicheng.note: Seat of Liang province, the Ma family's country.

chencang.note: The fort that stops Zhuge Liang's second northern expedition, ch. 97.

qishan.note: The road Zhuge Liang takes north again and again.

jieting.note: Ma Su loses it; Zhuge Liang weeps and executes him, ch. 96.

henei.note: Henei, north of the Yellow River opposite Luoyang. Wang Kuang's coalition contingent musters here.

gucheng.note: Where Zhang Fei, believing Guan Yu a turncoat, makes him kill a messenger to prove himself, ch. 28.

tanxi.note: The stream Liu Bei's horse Dilu leaps in a single bound, ch. 34.

longzhong.note: Zhuge Liang's farm. Liu Bei calls three times, ch. 37-38.

wulin.note: The north bank at Red Cliffs, where Cao Cao's fleet burned.

huarong.note: The narrow road where Guan Yu lets Cao Cao go, ch. 50.

leiyang.note: The county Pang Tong governs in a single morning, drunk, ch. 57.

luocheng.note: The siege where Pang Tong is killed, ch. 63.

fuguan.note: The gate into Yi province that Liu Bei takes by treachery, ch. 62.

tiandang.note: Huang Zhong's first Hanzhong victory, ch. 70.

yiling.note: Where Lu Xun burns Liu Bei's seven hundred li of camps, ch. 84.

lushui.note: The pestilential river Zhuge Liang crosses into Meng Huo's country, ch. 88.

tazhong.note: Where Jiang Wei is farming, in internal exile, when Wei invades, ch. 115.

yinping.note: The trackless mountain road Deng Ai takes to bypass Jiange, ch. 117.

mumen.note: Zhang He rides into the ambush that kills him, ch. 101.

shangfang.note: Sima Yi is trapped and burning when the rain comes, ch. 103.

suanzao.note: The allied camp at Suanzao where the coalition against Dong Zhuo swears its oath, ch. 5.

changjiang.note: The Great River. The line Cao Cao could not cross in ch. 43-50, and the frontier of Wu for seventy years.

huanghe.note: The Yellow River. Guandu, Baima and Yanjin are all fought along it.

hanshui._within: Natural Earth calls the Korean Han river 'Han' too, and without this it gets drawn near Seoul labelled 漢水.
hanshui.note: Xiangyang stands on it and Fancheng across it; Guan Yu drowns seven armies with it in ch. 74.

weishui.note: The Guanzhong corridor. Ma Chao at Tong Pass, ch. 58; Zhuge Liang's last camp at Wuzhangyuan, ch. 102.

huaishui.note: The Wei-Wu frontier east of the mountains. Shouchun and Hefei sit on its line.

xiangshui.note: Southern Jing province. The four commanderies Liu Bei takes in ch. 52-53 lie along it.

ganshui.note: The road south out of Wu.

jialing.note: The road from Hanzhong down into Yi province.

minjiang._within: Fujian's 閩江 is also romanized Min, and is a different character and a different river.

liaoshui.note: The far north-east, and the Gongsun family's moat.

fenshui.note: Bing province. Lü Bu's country, and the road the Xiongnu come down.

chapters.title: Three Heroes Swear Brotherhood in the Peach Garden; One Victory Shatters the Rebels at Julu
summary: The empire, long divided, must unite. Under the boy emperor Ling the eunuchs rule and the harvests fail, and a Daoist healer named Zhang Jue turns a following of five hundred thousand into an army wearing yellow headscarves.

In Zhuo county a call goes out for volunteers. Three men meet before the notice board: a mat-weaver who claims imperial descent, a fugitive who killed a bully in his home county, and a butcher and wine-seller with a voice like thunder. In a peach garden behind the butcher's house they swear to die on the same day.
They raise five hundred men, ride south, and break a Yellow Turban force outside Zhuo. The rebellion is far larger than they are.
chapters.history: Zhang Jue's rising is historical, and so is its scale. The oath in the peach garden is not — the histories say only that Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei 'slept on the same mat and were as brothers'.

pins.note: Reading the call for volunteers outside the county gate.
A fugitive from Hedong, five years on the run.
Owns the peach garden, and the wine.
General of Heaven, at the head of the rising.
Marching against Zhang Jue in the north.
A colonel of the palace guard, thirty years old.
Still a frontier general in the west.

chapters.title: Zhang Fei Whips the Government Inspector; He Jin Plots to Kill the Eunuchs
summary: The rebellion is broken and the brothers are given a county post so small it is an insult. When a government inspector arrives demanding a bribe, Zhang Fei ties him to a post and flogs him with a willow switch, and the three of them are fugitives again.

At court the Emperor Ling dies. The General-in-Chief He Jin, a butcher's son raised by his sister's place in the harem, resolves to destroy the ten eunuchs who run the palace — and is talked into summoning the frontier armies to help him do it.
chapters.history: The flogging is the novel's invention, and a characteristic one: the histories give the deed to Liu Bei, who is a good deal less genial than the story lets him be.

pins.note: A county magistrate, briefly.
Flogs the inspector and takes to the road.
Summoning the frontier generals to the capital.
Urging He Jin on.
Alone in warning that this will end badly.
Receives the summons east.
Dies of illness; his brothers are hunted down.

chapters.title: Dong Zhuo Rebukes the Emperor at Wenming Garden; Li Su Tempts Lü Bu with Red Hare
summary: The eunuchs strike first: He Jin is cut down inside the palace gate. Yuan Shao and Cao Cao storm in and kill every beardless man they find, two thousand of them, and in the confusion the boy emperor is carried out of the burning capital into the dark.
It is Dong Zhuo who finds him on the road, and Dong Zhuo who brings him back — with an army from Liang province and no intention of leaving. Within days he is talking openly of setting the boy aside.
Ding Yuan opposes him, protected by his formidable adopted son. Dong Zhuo sends a horse worth a thousand pieces of gold, and Lü Bu brings him Ding Yuan's head.
chapters.history: Dong Zhuo's march on Luoyang and the massacre of the eunuchs are historical. Red Hare is real too; the story that Lü Bu was bought with it is the novel's.

pins.note: Arrives with the Liang province army and does not leave.
Kills his adoptive father Ding Yuan for a horse.
Murdered inside the palace gate.
Storms the palace; then quarrels with Dong Zhuo and rides for Bohai.
Nine years old, and about to be made emperor.

chapters.title: Deposing the Emperor, Dong Zhuo Installs Another; Cao Cao Presents a Sword and Flees
summary: Dong Zhuo deposes the young emperor, enthrones his nine-year-old brother as Emperor Xian, and has the mother and son poisoned. In council he answers objections by having the objector dragged out and killed.

Cao Cao takes a jewelled sword from Wang Yun and goes to Dong Zhuo's chamber to use it. Caught in the mirror's reflection, he kneels and presents the blade as a gift instead, then rides east before the story can be tested.

On the road he is sheltered by his father's sworn brother Lü Boshe, hears knives being sharpened, and kills the household — nine people — before he sees the pig tied up for the feast. He kills Lü Boshe too, on the road, to keep him from talking.
chapters.history: The sword and the mirror are the novel's. Cao Cao's flight is historical; so is a version of the killing at Lü Boshe's house, which even the sympathetic sources record.

pins.note: Fails to kill Dong Zhuo; rides east to raise an army.
Releases Cao Cao, rides with him, and leaves him after Lü Boshe.
Killed on the road with his whole household.
Enthroned at nine.
Lends the sword, and begins to wait.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Rallies the Lords; Three Heroes Fight Lü Bu at Hulao Pass
summary: Cao Cao's forged summons brings eighteen lords and their armies to the camp at Suanzao. They elect Yuan Shao their chief, swear an oath, and immediately begin to quarrel about supplies.

At Sishui Pass Dong Zhuo's champion Hua Xiong kills every man sent against him. A nameless bowman in Gongsun Zan's train asks to try; Cao Cao pours him wine to send him off; he returns with the head and the wine is still warm.
At Hulao Pass Lü Bu breaks every commander in turn until all three brothers ride at him at once, and even then he only withdraws.
chapters.history: The coalition existed and achieved almost nothing. Guan Yu never met Hua Xiong, who was killed by Sun Jian's troops, and the three-on-one at Hulao is pure novel — the most famous fight in the book has no history behind it at all.

pins.note: Elected commander of the alliance.
Forged the summons that raised it.
Leads the vanguard against Sishui Pass.
Arrives in Gongsun Zan's train, unranked.
Kills Hua Xiong before the wine cools.
Holds the pass until Guan Yu.
Fights all three brothers at once.
In charge of supply, and withholds it from Sun Jian.

chapters.title: Burning the Capital, Dong Zhuo Commits an Atrocity; Hiding the Seal, Sun Jian Breaks Faith
summary: Rather than hold Luoyang, Dong Zhuo burns it. Several million people are driven west along the road to Chang'an with cavalry at their backs; the imperial tombs are dug up for their grave goods; the city burns for days.
Sun Jian, first into the ruins, finds a woman's body in a palace well with a box at her neck, and in the box the Imperial Hereditary Seal. He swears an oath that he has nothing, and starts for home.
Yuan Shao, who has been told, tries to take it from him. The alliance breaks up without ever reaching Chang'an.
chapters.history: The burning of Luoyang and the forced migration are historical, and the histories are no gentler about them than the novel is. Sun Jian's discovery of the seal is recorded in one source and doubted by others.

pins.note: Burns the capital behind him.
Carried west with the court.
Finds the Imperial Seal in a well.
Pursues alone and is ambushed; the other lords will not follow.

chapters.title: Yuan Shao Fights Gongsun Zan at the Pan River; Sun Jian Crosses the Yangtze to Attack Liu Biao
summary: The alliance turns on itself. Yuan Shao takes Ji province by a trick and then meets Gongsun Zan at the bridge over the Pan River, where Gongsun Zan is unhorsed and about to die — and is saved by a young officer in white, a stranger, who gives his name as Zhao Yun of Changshan.
In the south, Yuan Shu goads Sun Jian into attacking Liu Biao. Sun Jian pursues too far into the hills at Xianshan and is crushed under a rockfall and a volley of arrows. He is thirty-seven.
chapters.history: Both battles are historical. Zhao Yun's arrival at the bridge is the novel's staging — a way of putting him on the board early, and in Liu Bei's line of sight.

pins.note: Takes Ji province, then fights Gongsun Zan at the bridge.
Unhorsed, and saved by a stranger.
First appearance: a young officer in white.
Killed in the hills south of Xiangyang, aged thirty-seven.
Seventeen, and now head of the family.

chapters.title: Wang Yun Lays the Chain Stratagem; Dong Zhuo Storms out of the Phoenix Pavilion
summary: Wang Yun, weeping alone in his garden at the state of the empire, finds his singing-girl Diaochan weeping too, and asks her to do a thing no army has managed.

He promises her to Lü Bu and then presents her to Dong Zhuo, and lets each of them find out. She plays them against each other with complete composure — a look here, a tear there — until Lü Bu, hidden in the Phoenix Pavilion, sees what he takes for proof, and Dong Zhuo hurls a halberd at his head.
chapters.history: Diaochan is fictional. The histories record only that Lü Bu had an affair with one of Dong Zhuo's maids and lived in fear of being found out — which was enough for Wang Yun to work with.

pins.note: Sets the chain stratagem in motion.
Promised to Lü Bu, given to Dong Zhuo.
Between the capital and his treasure fortress.

chapters.title: Lü Bu Kills the Tyrant; Li Jue and Guo Si Sack the Capital
summary: Lü Bu kills Dong Zhuo in the palace gateway, in front of the court, with the abdication decree still in his hand. The body is exposed in the market; a lamp is set in its navel and burns for days on its own fat.

Then Wang Yun refuses amnesty to Dong Zhuo's officers, and Jia Xu tells them the only remaining option: 'Go back and take Chang'an. If it fails you can run then.' It does not fail. Wang Yun is killed, Lü Bu is driven out to wander, and Li Jue and Guo Si divide the Emperor between them.
chapters.history: Almost all of this is historical, including the lamp. Jia Xu's advice is recorded, and later Chinese historians blamed him personally for another decade of war.

pins.note: Killed in the palace gateway.
Driven out; begins seven years of wandering.
Refuses the amnesty, and is killed for it.
Gives the advice that costs the empire another decade.
Changes captors again.

chapters.title: Ma Teng Raises Troops for the Throne; Cao Cao Marches to Avenge His Father
summary: Ma Teng and Han Sui come east out of Liang province in the Emperor's name and are beaten back. Cao Cao, meanwhile, takes Yan province, absorbs three hundred thousand surrendered Yellow Turbans into an army, and begins to look like a power.

He sends for his father. Tao Qian of Xuzhou provides an escort, the escort murders the old man for his baggage, and Cao Cao comes east swearing to put the whole province to the sword. He very nearly does.
chapters.history: The massacres in Xuzhou are historical and were enormous; the novel does not soften them. Sources disagree on whether Tao Qian ordered the killing or merely failed to prevent it.

pins.note: Takes Yan province and an army of surrendered rebels.
Joins Cao Cao.
Marches east for the Emperor and is beaten back.
His escort murders Cao Cao's father.

chapters.title: Liu Bei Rescues Kong Rong at Beihai; Lü Bu Defeats Cao Cao at Puyang
summary: Kong Rong, besieged in Beihai by rebels, is broken out by a single rider — Taishi Ci, repaying a kindness done to his mother — and then sends to Liu Bei for help. Liu Bei's reaction to being asked is the most revealing line he has: 'Does Kong Rong know there is a Liu Bei in the world?'
He goes on to Xuzhou to lift Cao Cao's siege, and finds it lifted for him: Lü Bu, prompted by Chen Gong, has taken Yan province while Cao Cao's back was turned, and Cao Cao must go home.
chapters.history: Historical in outline. The novel gives Liu Bei the rescue of both Beihai and Xuzhou; the record is thinner and less flattering to everyone.

pins.note: Rides to Beihai, then to Xuzhou.
Still Gongsun Zan's officer.
Besieged, and rescued.
Breaks the siege line alone.
Abandons the Xuzhou campaign to save his own province.
Seizes Yan province behind Cao Cao.
The mind behind the seizure.

chapters.title: Tao Qian Yields Xuzhou Three Times; Cao Cao Fights Lü Bu at a Great Battle
summary: Tao Qian, dying, tries three times to hand Xuzhou to Liu Bei, who three times refuses it, and accepts only when there is no one left to refuse to. It is the first territory he has ever held.

Cao Cao and Lü Bu tear Yan province apart between them. Cao Cao is nearly killed at Puyang, burned and unhorsed, and saved by Dian Wei; a locust year starves both armies into breaking off; and Lü Bu, beaten, goes to Xuzhou to ask shelter of Liu Bei — who gives it.
chapters.history: The three refusals are the novel elaborating a real handover into a set-piece about Liu Bei's character. The locust famine of 194 is historical and was as decisive as any battle.

pins.note: Accepts Xuzhou at the third asking.
Dies, having given the province away.
Nearly burned to death in the gate.
Carries him out.
Beaten by famine as much as by Cao Cao.

chapters.title: Li Jue and Guo Si Fight; the Emperor Flees East
summary: The two men who hold the capital between them fall out over a jar of wine and a jealous wife, and fight in the streets of Chang'an for months. One holds the Emperor; the other kidnaps the entire court to even the score.

The Emperor escapes east with a starving procession of officials, is caught at the Yellow River crossing, and reaches the ruins of Luoyang with almost nobody left. The court sets up in the burnt shell of the old capital and the ministers gather firewood themselves.
chapters.history: Historical, and the novel understates it if anything. The flight from Chang'an in 195-196 is one of the grimmest episodes of the period.

pins.note: Reaches the ruins of his capital with nothing.
One of the few who gets the Emperor out.
Watching the road from Luoyang.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Moves the Court to Xuchang; Lü Bu Takes Xuzhou by Night
summary: Cao Cao arrives at Luoyang, feeds the court, and proposes a move to Xuchang where the granaries are. The Emperor agrees, because there is nothing else to agree to. From this point Cao Cao issues orders in the Emperor's name and his rivals must either obey them or be rebels.

One such order sends Liu Bei against Yuan Shu. He goes, leaving Zhang Fei to hold Xuzhou; Zhang Fei gets drunk, whips his officer Cao Bao, and Cao Bao opens the gate to Lü Bu. Liu Bei comes back to nothing, and takes shelter in Xiaopei — from his own guest.
chapters.history: The move to Xuchang is the pivot of the whole period: whoever held the Emperor could make his wars legal. Lü Bu's seizure of Xuzhou is historical; the drunken flogging is the novel's explanation for it.

pins.note: Takes the Emperor to Xuchang, and the initiative with him.
Argued for the move.
Loses Xuzhou while away campaigning.
Lost the city drunk.
Takes Xuzhou from the man who sheltered him.

chapters.title: Taishi Ci Fights the Little Conqueror; Sun Ce Cuts Out a Kingdom
summary: Sun Ce pawns his father's Imperial Seal to Yuan Shu for three thousand men and crosses the Yangtze with them. In a year he has the whole south-east.

At Shenting he and Taishi Ci fight alone in the hills until Sun Ce has Taishi Ci's halberd and Taishi Ci has Sun Ce's helmet, and neither can throw the other; Sun Ce takes him prisoner later and makes him a friend the same day. He lets him go on his word to return, and everyone tells him he is a fool, and Taishi Ci comes back at noon exactly.
chapters.history: Substantially historical, including the release of Taishi Ci on parole. The seal was really used as security for the loan.

pins.note: Crosses the Yangtze with three thousand borrowed men.
Joins him with troops and grain; they are the same age.
Fights Sun Ce to a standstill, then serves him.
Fourteen.
Holds the Imperial Seal as security, and begins to have ideas.

chapters.title: Lü Bu Shoots the Halberd at the Gate; Cao Cao Is Defeated at the River Yu
summary: Yuan Shu sends an army against Liu Bei at Xiaopei. Lü Bu, who wants neither of them strong, plants his halberd a hundred and fifty paces off, announces that he will shoot the side-blade and both sides must then go home, and hits it. Everyone goes home.

At Wan, Zhang Xiu surrenders and then revolts in the night over Cao Cao's treatment of his uncle's widow. Cao Cao escapes on a borrowed horse; his eldest son and his nephew are killed; and Dian Wei holds the gate on foot with no armour and both arms broken until he dies standing up, and no one dares pass him even then.
Cao Cao's public mourning is for Dian Wei, not for his son.
chapters.history: The archery feat is recorded in the histories, which is more than can be said for most of the novel's famous shots. The disaster at Wan is historical in every particular, including Dian Wei's death at the gate.

pins.note: Shoots the halberd at a hundred and fifty paces.
Saved by the shot.
Sent to destroy Liu Bei; goes home instead.
Loses his son, his nephew and his bodyguard in one night.
Dies on his feet in the gateway.
Surrenders, then revolts.
Now advising Zhang Xiu.

chapters.title: Yuan Shu Takes the Imperial Title; Cao Cao Borrows a Head
summary: Yuan Shu declares himself emperor on the strength of a stolen seal and a folk rhyme, and everyone who might have supported him stops. A coalition forms almost instantly.

Marching against him with a shortage of grain, Cao Cao tells his quartermaster to issue short measures, waits for the army to start muttering, then has the man beheaded for embezzlement and posts his head with a notice. The army is satisfied. It is the coldest thing in the book, and he does it in the middle of a chapter about someone else's treason.
chapters.history: Yuan Shu's usurpation destroyed him, as the novel says. The borrowed head is recorded in a commentary to the histories and the novel reproduces it almost unchanged.

pins.note: Declares himself emperor, and is abandoned.
Borrows his quartermaster's head.
Joins the coalition against Yuan Shu.
Breaks with Yuan Shu over the title.

chapters.title: Jia Xu Foresees a Victory; Xiahou Dun Eats His Own Eye
summary: Jia Xu, advising Zhang Xiu, tells him to pursue a retreating Cao Cao, and when that fails tells him to pursue again immediately — and is right both times, for reasons he explains afterwards with some patience.

Cao Cao turns on Lü Bu. At the siege lines Xiahou Dun takes an arrow through the left eye, pulls it out with the eyeball still on it, says 'the essence of my father and mother — I cannot throw it away', swallows it, and rides down the man who shot him.
chapters.history: Xiahou Dun really did lose an eye to an arrow and was called 'blind Xiahou' for it, to his lasting annoyance. Eating it is the novel's contribution.

pins.note: Right twice in a row, for reasons nobody else can see.
Turns on Lü Bu at last.
Loses an eye and swallows it.
Besieged.
Joins the siege.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Floods Xiapi; Lü Bu Dies at the White Gate Tower
summary: Cao Cao dams the Yi and the Si and lets them into the city. Lü Bu, who has stopped drinking and started forbidding it, alienates the last officers he has; they tie him up while he sleeps and open the gate.

At the White Gate Tower he offers to serve — 'you take the infantry, I will take the cavalry, and the empire is yours' — and Cao Cao wavers. He asks Liu Bei's opinion. Liu Bei says four words: 'Remember Ding Yuan and Dong Zhuo.' Lü Bu is strangled.
Chen Gong, offered his life, walks to the executioner without stopping. Zhang Liao curses everyone present and is untied by Cao Cao personally.
chapters.history: Historical, including Liu Bei's intervention — the one moment in the novel where his mildness drops entirely and he simply has a man killed.

pins.note: Strangled at the White Gate Tower.
Refuses his life.
Leaves the novel here without a word.
Curses his captors, and is spared.
'Remember Ding Yuan and Dong Zhuo.'

chapters.title: Cao Cao Hunts at Xutian; Dong Cheng Receives the Girdle Edict
summary: At the imperial hunt Cao Cao rides level with the Emperor, takes the Emperor's own bow to shoot the deer, and then keeps the bow. When the officers cheer the kill, he moves in front of the Emperor to receive it. Guan Yu reaches for his blade and Liu Bei stops him with a look.

That night the Emperor bites his finger and writes an edict in blood, sews it into a jade girdle, and gives the girdle to his father-in-law Dong Cheng as a gift, in public, with Cao Cao watching. Seven men eventually sign it. One of them is Liu Bei, who immediately starts growing vegetables to look harmless.
chapters.history: The girdle edict and Dong Cheng's conspiracy are historical, and so is its failure. The hunt at Xutian is the novel's staging of what the conspiracy was about.

pins.note: Takes the Emperor's bow, and keeps it.
Writes the edict in his own blood.
Receives the girdle.
Signs, then grows vegetables.
Reaches for his blade at the hunt.
Signs the edict and rides home.
Has finished Gongsun Zan and turns south.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Discusses Heroes over Warm Wine; Guan Yu Takes Xuzhou by a Ruse
summary: Cao Cao invites Liu Bei to eat green plums and drink warmed wine, and asks him to name the heroes of the age. Liu Bei names everyone he can think of; Cao Cao dismisses them all and says: 'The only heroes in the world are you and I.' Liu Bei drops his chopsticks — and is saved by a thunderclap, which lets him pretend to be a man frightened of storms.
He gets himself sent out of the capital on campaign and does not come back. Guan Yu kills the governor of Xuzhou at the gate, and the province is theirs again.
chapters.history: The conversation over plums is in the histories almost word for word, dropped chopsticks and all. It is the moment Cao Cao tells Liu Bei he knows exactly what he is.

pins.note: 'The only heroes in the world are you and I.'
Escapes the capital and takes Xuzhou back.
Kills Che Zhou at the gate.
Killed at the gate.
Preparing to come south.

chapters.title: Yuan Shao and Cao Cao Both Take the Field; Chen Lin's Proclamation Cures a Headache
summary: Yuan Shao moves south at last with an army the histories put at a hundred thousand. Chen Lin writes the denunciation that goes ahead of it, a document so comprehensively insulting about Cao Cao's ancestry that Cao Cao, reading it in bed with a migraine, sits up cured and laughing.
Liu Bei's recovered province does not last the season.
chapters.history: Chen Lin's proclamation survives and is as savage as the novel says. Cao Cao later spared him, on the grounds that he had been shooting at the right target.

pins.note: Marches south.
Writes the denunciation.
Cured of a headache by an insult.

chapters.title: Mi Heng Reviles the Traitor Naked; Ji Ping Is Tortured for a Poisoning
summary: The scholar Mi Heng, sent to insult Cao Cao, strips to the skin in open court and gives an accounting of every officer present. Cao Cao declines to kill him and sends him to Liu Biao instead, who sends him to Huang Zu, who does it — which was the intention all along.
The court physician Ji Ping, party to Dong Cheng's conspiracy, puts poison in Cao Cao's medicine. He is taken, tortured through a night, loses his fingers and his tongue, and names nobody.
chapters.history: Both are historical, and Cao Cao's use of a third party to kill Mi Heng is exactly as the novel gives it.

pins.note: Strips in open court, and is sent away to be killed by others.
Tortured through a night; names nobody.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Kills the Empress; Liu Bei Flees to Yuan Shao
summary: The girdle conspiracy is discovered. Dong Cheng and his fellow signatories are executed with their households, and the pregnant Empress Dong is dragged out of the palace and strangled in front of the Emperor, who is told to be quiet.
Cao Cao then falls on Xuzhou. The brothers are scattered in a night: Zhang Fei into the hills, Liu Bei north to Yuan Shao, and Guan Yu cut off on a hill with Liu Bei's wives.
chapters.history: The purge of Dong Cheng's conspiracy is historical, including the killing of the Emperor's pregnant consort.

pins.note: Executed with his household.
Watches his consort strangled.
Breaks Xuzhou and scatters the brothers.
Flees north to the enemy.
Cut off on a hill with his brother's wives.
Vanishes into the hills.

chapters.title: Guan Yu Surrenders on Three Conditions; He Kills Yan Liang to Repay a Kindness
summary: Surrounded, Guan Yu surrenders — to the Han, not to Cao Cao; the wives to be maintained in their own household; and leave to go the moment he learns where Liu Bei is. Cao Cao accepts all three, and then spends months trying to buy him with a title, a fortune, gowns, feasts and Red Hare.

Guan Yu takes the horse, because it will carry him to his brother faster. When Yan Liang's champions are killing everyone Cao Cao sends against them, Guan Yu rides down the slope, splits Yan Liang before he can rise, and comes back with the head.
chapters.history: The three conditions are the novel's. The killing of Yan Liang is historical and was exactly this abrupt.

pins.note: Surrenders on three conditions, then kills Yan Liang.
Killed before he can rise.
Cannot buy him, and knows it.
Carries the terms.
In the enemy camp, watching his brother fight for the wrong side.

chapters.title: Yuan Shao Loses a Second Champion; Guan Yu Hangs Up His Seal and Goes
summary: Wen Chou goes the way of Yan Liang. Yuan Shao, having now lost both his best men to a man riding under Cao Cao's banner, twice orders Liu Bei's execution and is twice talked out of it.

Then a letter reaches Guan Yu telling him where his brother is. He seals up every gift he has been given, leaves the inventory on the table with his seal of office on top, and rides out with the two carriages. Cao Cao will not allow pursuit.
chapters.history: Historical in outline, and the histories agree on the detail that matters: he left the rewards behind.

pins.note: Hangs up his seal and leaves the gifts behind.
Killed.
Forbids pursuit.
Twice nearly executed by his own host.

chapters.title: Riding Alone a Thousand Li; Five Passes and Six Commanders
summary: Guan Yu has no travel warrant, and every gate between him and his brother is shut. He forces five passes in succession and kills six commanders doing it, escorting two carriages the whole way, and stopping to be polite to each garrison before he kills its officer.
chapters.history: Entirely fictional — a set-piece invented for the novel. Guan Yu's real journey was unopposed, because Cao Cao had said to let him go.

pins.note: Five passes, six commanders, two carriages.
Joins him on the road.

chapters.title: Zhang Fei Doubts His Brother at Gucheng; the Oath Is Made Good
summary: Zhang Fei, holding a small town, hears that Guan Yu is coming and rides out to kill him — convinced he has sold himself to Cao Cao. Guan Yu is given the time it takes a drum to beat three times to prove otherwise, and a pursuing Cao Cao officer arrives at exactly the right moment to lose his head.
The brothers are together again, with Zhao Yun joining them at last, and Guan Ping and Zhou Cang picked up on the road. It has taken them the better part of a year to find each other.
chapters.history: Gucheng is the novel's. The reunion is real; the drumbeat is theatre.

pins.note: Given three drumbeats to prove himself.
Rides out to kill him.
Slips away from Yuan Shao.
Joins Liu Bei for good.

chapters.title: The Little Conqueror Executes a Daoist; Sun Quan Inherits the South-East
summary: Sun Ce has the Daoist Yu Ji executed for the crime of being more beloved than himself, and is haunted to death for it — starting at his own reflection, tearing open a healing arrow wound, dead at twenty-six.
He leaves the south-east to his eighteen-year-old brother with the clearest advice in the book: for matters of the field, ask Zhou Yu; for holding what we have, ask Zhang Zhao.
chapters.history: Sun Ce really did die at twenty-six of an assassin's arrow wound. The haunting is the novel's explanation for a death that was otherwise merely unlucky.

pins.note: Dead at twenty-six.
Eighteen, and now responsible for all of it.
Comes at once.
Executed, and does not stay dead.

chapters.title: Yuan Shao Loses Guandu; the Granaries at Wuchao Burn
summary: The armies lock at Guandu and Cao Cao, outnumbered and nearly out of grain, is close to withdrawing. Then Xu You, insulted once too often by Yuan Shao, walks into his camp at midnight — and Cao Cao comes out barefoot to meet him.

Xu You gives him the location of the granaries. Cao Cao burns Wuchao that night with five thousand men wearing Yuan Shao's colours, and by morning the largest army in China is starving and coming apart. It never recovers.
chapters.history: The decisive battle of northern China, and the novel follows the record closely, including Cao Cao's bare feet.

pins.note: Outnumbered, out of grain, and one defection from winning.
Loses the north in a night.
Walks over at midnight with the location of the granaries.
Writes the letter telling him to hold.
Goes over to Cao Cao.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Breaks Yuan Shao at Cangting; Liu Bei Takes Shelter with Liu Biao
summary: Yuan Shao, ill and diminished, is beaten again at Cangting and goes home to die of it. Cao Cao turns on Liu Bei, who has nowhere left in the north to stand.
He goes south to Liu Biao, a distant kinsman, who receives him warmly and gives him the border town of Xinye — which is to say, puts him between Jing province and Cao Cao.
chapters.history: Historical. Liu Bei's seven years at Xinye are the longest he stays anywhere before Yi province.

pins.note: Beaten a second time, and dying.
Given a border town to be a shield.
Receives his kinsman, and uses him.

chapters.title: The Yuan Brothers Fight over the Inheritance; Ye Falls
summary: Yuan Shao dies and his sons immediately begin fighting each other over what is left, which saves Cao Cao the trouble of fighting them together. Ye is besieged, flooded and taken; Shen Pei is executed facing north, towards his dead lord.
Cao Pi finds Yuan Xi's wife, the Lady Zhen, among the captives and takes her for himself, which his father permits.
chapters.history: Historical, including the fratricide, the flooding of Ye, and Cao Pi's acquisition of the Lady Zhen.

pins.note: Takes Yuan Shao's capital.
At war with his own brother.
Executed facing north.
Takes the Lady Zhen.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Pacifies the North; Guo Jia Wins a Campaign after His Own Death
summary: The last Yuan brothers flee to Liaodong. Cao Cao does not pursue: on the advice Guo Jia left behind him, sealed, he simply halts and waits — and Gongsun Kang, calculating that two guests are more dangerous than one enemy, sends their heads down instead.
Guo Jia dies on the road home at thirty-seven. Cao Cao mourns him harder than he mourned his own son.
chapters.history: The posthumous stratagem is historical, and so is Cao Cao's grief. He would say after Red Cliffs that if Guo Jia had lived it would not have happened.

pins.note: Halts, and lets the frontier do his killing.
Dies at thirty-seven, having won one more campaign in a sealed letter.
Sends the heads down.

chapters.title: The Leap at the Tan Stream
summary: Liu Biao's wife's family decide to be rid of Liu Bei at a banquet. Warned mid-course, he goes over the wall to his horse and finds the road blocked by the Tan Stream, deep and fast and thirty feet across.
The horse Dilu, which he has been warned is unlucky and will one day kill its master, gathers itself and clears it.
chapters.history: The leap is legend rather than record, and the novel knows it — the whole point of Dilu is the prophecy it is busy contradicting.

pins.note: Clears thirty feet of water on an unlucky horse.
Arranges the banquet.

chapters.title: Water Mirror Names Two Men; Shan Fu Comes to Xinye
summary: Sheltering overnight with the recluse Sima Hui, Liu Bei is told the reason he has spent twenty years losing: he has soldiers and no strategist. 'Sleeping Dragon or Young Phoenix — either one of them would be enough to settle the empire.' He will not say who they are.
Shortly afterwards a singing madman on the road turns out to be a strategist calling himself Shan Fu, and Liu Bei's fortunes change within the month.
chapters.history: Sima Hui and the two nicknames are historical. The novel arranges them into a prophecy that the next ten chapters spend cashing in.

pins.note: 'Sleeping Dragon or Young Phoenix would be enough.'
Arrives calling himself Shan Fu.

chapters.title: Xu Shu Is Taken by a Forged Letter, and Names His Successor
summary: Shan Fu — really Xu Shu — beats Cao Ren twice in a fortnight, which tells Cao Cao exactly who he is dealing with. Cao Cao therefore takes his mother, and forges her handwriting to call him north.

He goes, because he is a son. His mother, learning why he came, hangs herself for the shame of it. Riding away he turns back once, to tell Liu Bei the name of the man in the thatched cottage at Longzhong.
chapters.history: Historical, including the forged letter. The novel adds the mother's suicide, and the recommendation on the road.

pins.note: Goes north to a forged letter, and names Zhuge Liang on the way out.
Forges a mother's hand.
Beaten twice in a fortnight.
Farming, and waiting.

chapters.title: Twice to the Thatched Cottage, and Twice Turned Away
summary: Liu Bei rides to Longzhong and finds the man out. He rides again through snow and finds his brother instead. Guan Yu thinks it beneath him and Zhang Fei wants to tie the man up and carry him back; Liu Bei goes a third time in the spring.
chapters.history: The three visits are historical, and were remembered as extraordinary precisely because a general did not do this.

pins.note: Calls twice, and is not received.
Thinks it beneath him.
Offers to fetch the man with rope.
Out, both times.

chapters.title: The Longzhong Plan; Sun Quan Avenges His Father at Last
summary: At the third asking Zhuge Liang receives him, and lays out on a map the shape of the next seventy years: Cao Cao holds the north and cannot be fought head-on; Sun Quan holds the river and should be an ally, not a target; Jing and Yi provinces are weakly held by men who cannot keep them; take those two, hold the passes, wait for the north to falter, and come out in two columns.
Meanwhile Sun Quan finally kills Huang Zu, and the head that killed his father goes on his father's altar.
chapters.history: The Longzhong Plan is historical and is close to the novel's version. It also very nearly worked.

pins.note: Lays out the next seventy years on a map.
Comes a third time.
Kills Huang Zu at last.
Changes sides, and brings the river with him.
Killed; his head goes on Sun Jian's altar.

chapters.title: Bowang Burns: the Sleeping Dragon's First Battle
summary: Guan Yu and Zhang Fei are not persuaded by a twenty-seven-year-old in a carriage until Xiahou Dun's ten thousand come up the Bowang road, are drawn into a defile, and are set alight from both sides. After that they take their orders without comment.
chapters.history: The Bowang ambush happened, but Liu Bei ran it himself, several years before Zhuge Liang joined him. The novel hands his subordinate the credit to make an entrance of it.

pins.note: Wins his first battle without drawing a sword.
Walks into the defile.
Stops arguing.

chapters.title: Xinye Is Burned and Abandoned; Cao Cao Comes South
summary: Liu Biao dies. His younger son surrenders Jing province by letter without telling anyone, and is rewarded with a governorship far away and murdered on the road to it.
Zhuge Liang burns Xinye behind them and Liu Bei goes south — with a hundred thousand civilians who will not stay behind, moving at ten li a day, with Cao Cao's cavalry coming on at three hundred.
chapters.history: The surrender of Jing and the flight south are historical. So, remarkably, is the crowd: Liu Bei really did refuse to abandon the people who followed him, and it nearly killed him.

pins.note: Surrenders the province by letter, and is killed for it.
Dies.
Takes Jing province without a battle.
Burns the town and moves at ten li a day.
Holds Jiangxia, and a way out.

chapters.title: Zhao Yun Alone at Changban; Liu Bei Throws His Son on the Ground
summary: The column is caught and destroyed. Zhao Yun goes back into it alone, three times, and comes out at evening with Liu Bei's infant son inside his armour, having cut through the whole of Cao Cao's centre — who were under orders to take him alive, because Cao Cao wanted him.
Liu Bei takes the child and throws it on the ground: 'For the sake of this infant I nearly lost a great commander.'
chapters.history: Zhao Yun really did bring the child out. Throwing it down is the novel's, and readers have argued for six centuries about whether it is sincere.

pins.note: Goes back into the army three times.
Throws the child on the ground.
An infant, carried out inside armour.
Orders him taken alive, and so loses him.

chapters.title: Zhang Fei Holds the Bridge Alone; Liu Qi Takes Them Off the River
summary: Zhang Fei stands at the far end of the Changban bridge with twenty riders, has them drag brushwood behind the treeline to raise dust, and shouts three times. An army stops. A man beside Cao Cao dies of fright. Then Zhang Fei pulls the bridge down, which tells Cao Cao he was bluffing — but by then Liu Qi's boats have taken them off the bank.
chapters.history: Historical in its essentials, including the twenty riders and the dust. The novel adds the man frightened to death.

pins.note: Twenty riders, some brushwood, and three shouts.
Takes them off the bank.
Goes to make an alliance out of nothing.

chapters.title: The Sleeping Dragon Debates the Scholars of Wu
summary: Zhuge Liang crosses to Chaisang with nothing to offer and one thing to sell: the idea that Sun Quan can fight. Zhang Zhao and the civil officers, who want to surrender and keep their offices, take him apart one at a time in open court, and he answers all of them.
He then goes to Sun Quan and does not argue at all. He observes that if Wu cannot fight, Wu should certainly surrender — and watches the young man's face change.
chapters.history: The embassy is historical; the debate is the novel's finest set-piece and almost entirely invented.

pins.note: Sells a war to a court that wants to surrender.
Leads the party for surrender.
Brought him across.

chapters.title: Zhuge Liang Provokes Zhou Yu with a Poem
summary: Zhou Yu, who has already decided on war, pretends otherwise to see what Zhuge Liang is made of. Zhuge Liang suggests that the whole thing could be settled by sending Cao Cao two women — and recites a line from Cao Zhi's poem about the Bronze Bird Terrace naming the two Qiao.
One of them is Sun Ce's widow. The other is Zhou Yu's wife. Zhou Yu comes off his seat swearing to fight.
chapters.history: The poem predates the terrace and says nothing of the kind; the novel is misreading it on purpose, and Zhou Yu — who had decided on war days earlier — is letting himself be moved.

pins.note: Provoked, entirely willingly.
Misquotes a poem on purpose.
Cuts the corner off his desk to end the argument.
Builds a fleet he does not understand.

chapters.title: Jiang Gan Carries a Letter Home; Cao Cao Beheads His Own Admirals
summary: Cao Cao's fleet is handled by two surrendered Jing province admirals — the only men in his army who understand the river. Zhou Yu, visited by an old schoolfellow now working for Cao Cao, gets drunk on purpose, leaves a forged letter where it will be found, and talks in his sleep.
Jiang Gan steals the letter and rides home with it. Cao Cao has both admirals executed before the ink is dry, and understands what he has done about a minute afterwards.
chapters.history: Invented. But the two admirals were real, and Cao Cao really did lose the only competent naval officers he had.

pins.note: Talks in his sleep, loudly.
Executed on a forged letter.
Kills the only two men who understood the river.

chapters.title: Straw Boats Borrow Arrows; Huang Gai Asks to Be Beaten
summary: Zhou Yu, who would rather Zhuge Liang were dead than allied, orders him to produce a hundred thousand arrows in three days. Zhuge Liang agrees to do it in two, takes twenty boats stuffed with straw and screened with cloth out into the fog, drums at Cao Cao's camp until they are stuck full, and comes home thanking him for the loan.
Then Huang Gai proposes to be flogged nearly to death in open council, so that his defection will be believed.
chapters.history: Both are famous and both are fiction. The arrow episode is borrowed from a real incident involving Sun Quan and moved wholesale to a better character.

pins.note: Borrows a hundred thousand arrows and returns none.
Sets an impossible task, and is answered.
Asks to be flogged.
Lends the arrows.

chapters.title: Pang Tong Chains the Fleet Together
summary: Cao Cao's northern soldiers are seasick and dying. Pang Tong, arriving as a friendly scholar, offers the obvious remedy: chain the ships together in ranks and plank them over, and the fleet becomes as steady as dry land.
It works exactly as promised. It also makes the fleet one object, which cannot be moved and cannot be separated.
chapters.history: Pang Tong was real and Cao Cao's ships were linked; whether anyone talked him into it is the novel's contribution.

pins.note: Sells him a cure that is also a trap.
Chains his fleet into one target.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Sings on the Yangtze and Kills a Man for Saying So
summary: The night before the battle Cao Cao holds a banquet on the water, takes a spear, and sings his own poem to the moon — 'the moon is bright, the stars are few, the crows fly south'. An officer remarks that crows flying south at night is an ill omen on the eve of a battle. Cao Cao runs him through with the spear, and goes on singing.
He apologises in the morning and buries him well.
chapters.history: The poem is Cao Cao's own and survives. The killing is the novel's, and it is placed here to remind you what he is on the night before he loses.

pins.note: Sings, and kills a man for listening carefully.
Waiting for wind.

chapters.title: Praying for the East Wind
summary: Everything is ready and the wind is wrong: in the eleventh month it blows from the north-west, and a fire-attack would burn Wu's own fleet. Zhou Yu takes to his bed with an illness no physician can name, and Zhuge Liang writes him a prescription of sixteen characters — and undertakes to borrow three days of south-east wind.
He builds an altar, goes up it in Daoist robes, and at midnight the wind changes. He is off the altar and gone downriver before Zhou Yu's assassins reach the top step.
chapters.history: The wind change is real meteorology — a winter monsoon reversal that a Yangtze sailor could have predicted. The altar is the novel's, and it is what turned Zhuge Liang from a strategist into a wizard in the popular imagination.

pins.note: Borrows three days of south-east wind, and leaves before he can be thanked.
Ill of a wind direction.
Sails with oil and kindling under the hatches.
Waiting downstream with a boat.

chapters.title: Red Cliffs Burns; Guan Yu Lets Cao Cao Go at Huarong
summary: Huang Gai's squadron comes in under a false flag with the wind behind it, fires the leading ships, and the chained fleet cannot scatter. The river burns from bank to bank. Cao Cao loses an army that had never been beaten and runs north through the marshes with a few hundred men, laughing twice at his enemies' stupidity and being ambushed both times.

At the Huarong road Guan Yu is waiting with orders to kill him — and Cao Cao reminds him of the horse, the gowns, and the passes he was let through. Guan Yu turns his horse aside and lets the whole column pass.
chapters.history: The battle and the fire are historical; Cao Cao's escape through the marshes is too. The meeting at Huarong is invented — the novel's way of paying off Guan Yu's debt and setting the ledger straight before he dies.

pins.note: Sails in under a false flag.
Wins the battle of the age at thirty-three.
Loses an army, and laughs twice too often.
Lets him go, and pays for it later.
Gave him the orders knowing he would disobey them.
Gets him out.

chapters.title: Zhou Yu Fights Cao Ren for Nan Commandery; Zhuge Liang Walks In Behind Him
summary: Zhou Yu spends a season and an arrow through the ribs prising Cao Ren out of Nan commandery, and comes up to the walls to find Zhao Yun already on them, holding the city with the seals Zhuge Liang collected while the fighting was going on elsewhere.
Jiangling, Xiangyang's southern approaches and the four commanderies below the river all change hands in a fortnight, and none of them to Wu. The alliance never entirely recovers.
chapters.history: The quarrel over Jing province is historical and is the true beginning of the Wu-Shu enmity that eventually kills Guan Yu.

pins.note: Takes an arrow, and then loses the city anyway.
Driven out of Nan commandery.
On the walls before Wu arrives.
Collects the seals while others do the fighting.

chapters.title: Zhao Yun Takes Guiyang and Declines the Governor's Sister-in-Law
summary: The southern commanderies fall one after another. At Guiyang the surrendering governor offers Zhao Yun his widowed sister-in-law along with the seals, and Zhao Yun refuses — on the grounds that the man is a new subordinate, that she is a widow, and that accepting would look exactly like what it would be.
chapters.history: Historical, and recorded because it was thought remarkable. Zhao Yun's reasoning in the sources is the same as the novel's.

pins.note: Takes the city and declines the marriage.
Watching the province go.

chapters.title: Guan Yu and Huang Zhong Decline to Kill Each Other; Zhang Liao Holds Xiaoyao Ford
summary: At Changsha the sixty-year-old Huang Zhong is unhorsed and Guan Yu will not strike him; the next day Huang Zhong, who never misses, puts his arrow through Guan Yu's helmet plume on purpose. Their governor tries to execute Huang Zhong for it, and Wei Yan kills the governor and opens the gates.

In the east Sun Quan attacks Hefei and Zhang Liao breaks him at Xiaoyao Ford with eight hundred men against ten thousand — a defeat so total that Wu mothers were said to quiet children with Zhang Liao's name.
chapters.history: Both are historical. Xiaoyao Ford was one of the great disasters of Sun Quan's career and he never entirely lived it down.

pins.note: Will not kill an unhorsed old man.
Shoots the plume off his helmet instead of his head.
Kills his own governor and opens the gate.
Broken by eight hundred men.
Eight hundred against ten thousand.
Cuts him out of the encirclement.

chapters.title: The Trap at Ganlu Temple Becomes a Wedding
summary: Zhou Yu's plan is to offer Sun Quan's sister to the widowed Liu Bei, hold him in Wu as a hostage-son-in-law, and trade him back for Jing province. Zhuge Liang sends him anyway with three sealed bags of instructions and Zhao Yun to open them.

Liu Bei charms the Dowager, who inspects him at Ganlu Temple and likes what she sees, and the sham marriage becomes a real one over Zhou Yu's objections. The bride keeps a hundred armed maids in her bedchamber.
chapters.history: The marriage is historical and so is Lady Sun's armed household, which the sources say frightened Liu Bei considerably.

pins.note: Walks into the trap and marries out of it.
Keeps a hundred armed maids in her rooms.
Carrying three sealed bags.
Whose plan this was.

chapters.title: Zhou Yu Loses the Lady and the Army Too
summary: Liu Bei, comfortable in Wu and losing interest in leaving, is prodded out of it by the second sealed bag. He and his wife go over the border at New Year with pursuit behind them, and Lady Sun stops the pursuing officers herself — they are her brother's men and she is her mother's daughter, and they let her through.

Zhou Yu's own troops, catching them at the bank, are met by Zhuge Liang's boats and a chant from the far shore: the Chief Commander's grand scheme has lost him the lady and the army too. He coughs blood.
chapters.history: The escape is historical. The taunting chant is the novel's, and it is the line Zhou Yu is remembered by.

pins.note: Goes over the border at New Year.
Faces down her brother's officers herself.
Coughs blood on the riverbank.
Waiting with boats and a chant.

chapters.title: The Bronze Bird Terrace; Zhou Yu's Third Scheme
summary: Cao Cao opens his great terrace at Ye with an archery contest and a banquet, and is presented with a memorial urging him to take the imperial title. He declines, in language that leaves the question open.

Zhou Yu tries once more: Wu will march west and take Yi province for Liu Bei, if Liu Bei will let the army pass through Jing on the way. Zhuge Liang thanks him warmly and prepares an ambush at every ford.
chapters.history: The terrace is real and Cao Zhi's poem for its opening survives. The 'borrow a road' scheme is the novel's.

pins.note: Opens his terrace, and declines the throne in a way that invites asking again.
Writes the poem for the opening.
Asks to borrow a road.
Thanks him, and mines the fords.

chapters.title: Zhou Yu Dies at Baqiu; the Young Phoenix Governs a County in a Morning
summary: Zhou Yu's third scheme fails like the others, and the wound reopens. He dies at thirty-six at Baqiu, and his last words are a complaint to heaven: 'Since it made me, why did it also make Liang?'

Zhuge Liang attends the funeral and delivers a eulogy so sincere that Wu's officers cannot bring themselves to kill him at it. On the way home he recruits Pang Tong, whom Sun Quan has rejected for being ugly and Liu Bei has parked in a small county — where he clears a hundred days of arrears in one morning, drunk, to make a point.
chapters.history: Zhou Yu died at thirty-six on campaign. The rivalry with Zhuge Liang, and the dying complaint, are the novel's invention: the histories show them barely interacting, and Zhou Yu magnanimous.

pins.note: 'Since it made me, why did it also make Liang?'
Weeps at the funeral of a man he outmanoeuvred.
Succeeds him, and keeps the alliance alive.
Clears a hundred days of arrears in one morning, drunk.

chapters.title: Ma Chao Avenges His Father; Cao Cao Cuts Off His Beard
summary: Cao Cao has Ma Teng killed at Xuchang, and Ma Chao comes down out of Liang province with the Qiang cavalry to settle it. At Tong Pass he breaks Cao Cao's army and chases him personally through his own men.
Cao Cao throws off his red cloak because they are calling for the man in red, cuts off his beard because they are calling for the man with the beard, and escapes wrapped in a flag.
chapters.history: Historical in outline, and the cloak and beard are recorded — though the sources put a little more dignity into it than the novel does.

pins.note: Comes down out of Liang province for his father.
Killed, which starts it.
Loses his cloak, his beard and nearly his life.
Gets him across the river under fire.

chapters.title: Xu Chu Fights Stripped to the Waist; a Letter Is Blotted on Purpose
summary: Xu Chu strips off his armour to fight Ma Chao and takes two arrows for it. Then Jia Xu ends the campaign without another battle: Cao Cao writes a friendly letter to Han Sui and smudges out the important passages himself before sending it.
Ma Chao reads it over Han Sui's shoulder, sees a letter that has been carefully edited, and concludes the obvious wrong thing. The coalition destroys itself within the week.
chapters.history: The altered letter is in the histories and is Jia Xu at his most characteristic: he wins by handing the enemy something to misread.

pins.note: Fights stripped to the waist, and takes two arrows.
Reads a letter, and destroys his own alliance.
Wins the campaign with an inkbrush.
Takes the north-west.

chapters.title: Zhang Song Offers the Map of Shu
summary: Liu Zhang, frightened of Zhang Lu in Hanzhong and of Cao Cao behind him, sends Zhang Song to Xuchang to ask for help. Cao Cao, who has just beaten Ma Chao and is in no mood to be polite to an ugly little man from the provinces, humiliates him and throws him out.
Zhang Song had come with a map of every road, ford and granary in Yi province in his sleeve, intending to give it to Cao Cao. He gives it to Liu Bei instead, and invites him in.
chapters.history: Historical, including the map and the humiliation. Cao Cao lost the west by being rude to a man he did not think mattered.

pins.note: Offers the map to one man, is insulted, and gives it to another.
Throws out the man carrying Yi province in his sleeve.
Invited in through the front door.
Asks for the help that destroys him.
Argues against letting him in.

chapters.title: Zhao Yun Stops a Boat on the River; Sun Quan and Cao Cao Face Each Other at Ruxu
summary: Lady Sun is recalled to Wu and takes Liu Bei's small son with her. Zhao Yun and Zhang Fei catch the boat mid-river, and Zhao Yun takes the child out of her arms — the second time he has carried Liu Shan out of somewhere.

At Ruxu, Cao Cao looks across the water at Sun Quan's fleet drawn up in perfect order and says the line that follows Sun Quan through history: 'To have a son one would wish for one like Sun Zhongmou.'
chapters.history: Both historical, and Cao Cao's remark is recorded — it was meant as praise and as a complaint about his own sons.

pins.note: Leaves, and takes the child.
Takes Liu Shan out of a boat, having once taken him out of an army.
'To have a son one would wish for one like Sun Zhongmou.'

chapters.title: Liu Bei Takes the Fu Pass
summary: The pretence of alliance ends. Zhang Song's correspondence is discovered and he is executed with his whole family; Liu Bei, already inside the province as a guest, stops being one.
Pang Tong offers three plans — a fast one, a sound one and a slow one — and Liu Bei takes the middle. The Fu Pass falls, and with it the road to Chengdu.
chapters.history: Historical. The novel is unusually blunt about Liu Bei's conduct here, and lets Pang Tong tell him to his face that invading a kinsman who invited you in is not a righteous war.

pins.note: Stops being a guest.
Offers three plans, and is told to stop moralising.
Executed with his family.

chapters.title: Pang Tong Dies at Fallen Phoenix Slope; Zhang Fei Releases Yan Yan
summary: Pang Tong, whose Daoist name is Young Phoenix, rides into a defile called Fallen Phoenix Slope on Liu Bei's white horse — which he has swapped for out of courtesy — and is shot to pieces by archers who think they are killing Liu Bei. He is thirty-five.

Coming west with the relief army, Zhang Fei takes the veteran Yan Yan, who tells him to get on with the beheading. Zhang Fei unties him instead, and Yan Yan talks the whole western road into surrendering.
chapters.history: Pang Tong really was killed by an arrow at Luo. The name of the slope is the novel's, and it is the most nakedly literary thing in the book.

pins.note: Killed on a borrowed white horse at a place named for him.
Whose archers do it.
Unties a prisoner, and gains a road.
Tells him to get on with the beheading.
Sets out west, leaving Guan Yu to hold Jing.

chapters.title: Zhang Ren Is Taken at the Bridge and Will Not Kneel
summary: Zhuge Liang comes west and takes Zhang Ren by drawing him across a bridge and cutting it behind him. Offered service, Zhang Ren answers that a loyal officer does not serve two masters, and is executed at his own request. Liu Bei has him buried by the bridge.
Luocheng falls. There is nothing between the army and Chengdu but Ma Chao, who is coming down from the north — for Zhang Lu.
chapters.history: Zhang Ren was real and did refuse to surrender. The novel gives him the best death in the western campaign.

pins.note: 'A loyal officer does not serve two masters.'
Coming down for Zhang Lu, and about to change sides.

chapters.title: Ma Chao Comes Over; Liu Zhang Gives Up Yi Province
summary: Ma Chao and Zhang Fei fight at Jiameng from midday until torches are lit and neither can put the other down. Then Li Hui talks Ma Chao into changing sides — he has nowhere else to go, and Zhang Lu is already trying to have him killed.
Ma Chao rides to Chengdu's walls and calls up, and Liu Zhang surrenders the next day rather than see the city stormed. Liu Bei has a province at last, twenty-nine years after the peach garden.
chapters.history: Historical: Ma Chao's defection really did end the siege without a fight, because Liu Zhang's nerve broke at the sight of him.

pins.note: Changes sides, and ends a siege by arriving.
Fights him to a standstill by torchlight.
Surrenders rather than see the city stormed.
Has a province, twenty-nine years after the peach garden.
Who arranged most of it.

chapters.title: Guan Yu Goes to the Feast with a Single Blade; the Empress Is Killed
summary: Lu Su invites Guan Yu across the river to discuss the return of Jing province, with swordsmen behind the screens. Guan Yu comes with one blade and one boat, keeps hold of Lu Su's wrist through the whole banquet, and walks him down to the water as a shield.

At Xuchang the Empress Fu's letter asking her father to act against Cao Cao is found. She is dragged from behind a false wall by the hair and beaten to death; her two sons are poisoned; her family are killed to the hundredth degree.
chapters.history: The single-blade meeting is historical, though the sources give the nerve to Lu Su. The killing of Empress Fu is also historical, and the novel does not exaggerate it.

pins.note: One blade, one boat, and a firm grip on his host's wrist.
Walked down to the water as a shield.
Watches his wife dragged out by the hair.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Takes Hanzhong; Zhang Liao Breaks Wu at Xiaoyao Ford Again
summary: Zhang Lu's theocracy in Hanzhong falls. He seals the treasuries before he goes rather than burn them — a courtesy Cao Cao repays by treating him well.

Cao Cao now stands one range of mountains above Liu Bei's brand-new province, and Sima Yi urges him to go straight down into it. He declines, with the remark that a man who has Long should not covet Shu.
chapters.history: Historical, and the refusal is one of the great might-have-beens: Yi province was newly conquered and unsteady, and Cao Cao never got so close again.

pins.note: Seals the treasuries instead of burning them.
'A man who has Long should not covet Shu.'
Urges him to go down into Yi province at once.
One range of mountains away.

chapters.title: Gan Ning Raids a Camp with a Hundred Riders; Zuo Ci Torments Cao Cao
summary: Gan Ning takes a hundred men with white goose feathers in their helmets straight through Cao Cao's camp at midnight and comes back without losing one. Sun Quan: 'Cao Cao has his Zhang Liao. I have my Gan Xingba.'
At Xuchang the Daoist Zuo Ci makes a fool of Cao Cao at a banquet — producing perch out of an empty basin, oranges that are hollow, and finally himself, in every direction at once.
chapters.history: The hundred riders are historical. Zuo Ci is folklore, imported to show Cao Cao, at the height of his power, unable to catch one old man.

pins.note: A hundred riders, white feathers, and no losses.
'Cao Cao has his Zhang Liao. I have my Gan Xingba.'
Cannot be caught, executed, or got rid of.

chapters.title: Guan Lu Reads the Future; Five Officers Try to Burn the Capital
summary: The diviner Guan Lu tells Cao Cao's fortune with unpleasant accuracy and declines all reward. Five loyalist officers, taking his reading as a signal, raise a fire in Xuchang and try to kill Cao Cao during it.

It fails. Cao Cao assembles the entire court and orders those who helped put the fire out to stand on one side and those who stayed indoors on the other; then he executes everyone on the first side, on the grounds that they were carrying weapons.
chapters.history: The plot is historical. The trick with the two sides is the novel's, and it is the single most chilling thing Cao Cao does in the book.

pins.note: Reads the future accurately, and declines payment.
Executes the men who fought the fire.
Beginning to move on Hanzhong.

chapters.title: Zhang Fei Drinks His Way Through Zhang He; Huang Zhong Takes Mount Tiandang
summary: Zhang Fei, facing an opponent who will not come down off a mountain, camps in front of him and drinks for fifty days in plain view, until Zhang He comes down to take advantage of a drunkard — and finds that the man at the table is a straw figure.
Huang Zhong, now over sixty and tired of being called old, takes Mount Tiandang and its granaries by letting himself be underestimated for a fortnight.
chapters.history: Both are historical victories; the staged drunkenness is the novel's, and it is exactly the sort of joke Zhang Fei's reputation invites.

pins.note: Drinks in plain view for fifty days, out of straw.
Comes down to take advantage of a drunkard.
Over sixty, and tired of hearing about it.

chapters.title: Huang Zhong Kills Xiahou Yuan at Dingjun; Zhao Yun Opens His Gates
summary: Huang Zhong is talked into fighting by being told he is too old for it, takes the high ground above Dingjun, waits until the afternoon heat has emptied Xiahou Yuan's men of fight, and comes down the hill in one movement. Xiahou Yuan is cut from shoulder to waist before he can get his horse turned.

Zhao Yun, pursued back to his camp with a fraction of his men, orders the gates thrown open, the banners lowered and every man to stand silent. Cao Cao's pursuit halts at the open gate, decides it is an ambush, and is destroyed retreating.
chapters.history: Both historical. Liu Bei's comment on hearing of the victory was that he had wanted the commander, not the deputy — Xiahou Yuan was the better prize.

pins.note: Comes down the hill once, and that is enough.
Cut from shoulder to waist.
Opens his gates and stands silent.
Chose the hour.

chapters.title: Chicken Ribs: Cao Cao Gives Up Hanzhong and Kills His Secretary for Knowing It
summary: Cao Cao, stuck in a campaign he cannot win and will not admit to losing, gives the night's watchword as 'chicken ribs'. Yang Xiu, who has spent years demonstrating that he can read his master's mind, tells the camp to pack: there is no meat on a chicken rib but it is a shame to throw it away.
He is right, and Cao Cao has him executed for it. The army withdraws from Hanzhong a few days later, exactly as Yang Xiu predicted.
chapters.history: Historical, watchword and all. Yang Xiu had also been backing the wrong son in the succession, which the novel leaves in the background.

pins.note: Right once too often.
Withdraws, exactly as predicted.
Has the western passes.

chapters.title: Liu Bei Becomes King of Hanzhong; Guan Yu Moves on Fancheng
summary: Liu Bei takes the title King of Hanzhong, which is as far as he can go without saying the other word. Guan Yu is made first of the Five Tiger Generals, and objects to sharing the rank with Huang Zhong until it is explained to him carefully.
Then he crosses the river and moves on Fancheng, and for a few months the Longzhong plan is working exactly as drawn.
chapters.history: Historical. Guan Yu's irritation at Huang Zhong's promotion is recorded and is entirely in character.

pins.note: King of Hanzhong.
Crosses the river, and the plan is working.
Shut up in the city.

chapters.title: Pang De Brings His Own Coffin; the Seven Armies Drown
summary: Pang De comes to relieve Fancheng carrying a coffin, to make it clear he does not intend to come back, and puts an arrow into Guan Yu's arm.

Then the autumn rains come. Guan Yu, who has spent a fortnight quietly moving boats upstream, cuts the dykes on the Han. Seven armies drown in a night; Yu Jin surrenders from a treetop; Pang De fights on a raft until it capsizes and is executed still refusing to kneel.
chapters.history: Historical, including the flood — though the sources suggest Guan Yu exploited it rather than engineered it. The reputation it won him was enormous, and it is what frightened Wu into acting.

pins.note: Cuts the dykes, and drowns seven armies.
Brings a coffin, and uses it.
Surrenders from a treetop.
Discusses moving the capital away from him.

chapters.title: Hua Tuo Scrapes the Bone; Lü Meng Crosses the River in White
summary: The arrow wound is poisoned to the bone. Hua Tuo proposes to cut it open and scrape the bone clean, and Guan Yu declines the ropes and the post, plays a board game through the operation, and drinks and jokes while the blade grates.

Downriver, Lü Meng announces an illness and hands over to the young and harmless-seeming Lu Xun, who writes Guan Yu a flattering letter. The Jing garrisons are thinned to reinforce Fancheng — and Wu's soldiers come up the river dressed as white-robed merchants, take the beacon towers without a signal being lit, and Jing province falls without a battle.
chapters.history: The bone-scraping is in the histories, although Hua Tuo was dead by then. The white-clothed crossing is historical and is the most elegant operation of the entire war.

pins.note: Plays a board game while his bone is scraped.
Offers no ropes, and is not asked for any.
Takes the province dressed as a merchant.
Writes a flattering letter, and is believed.

chapters.title: Xu Huang Breaks the Siege; the Army Melts Away
summary: Xu Huang relieves Fancheng — an old friend of Guan Yu's, who talks with him pleasantly across the lines and then offers a reward for his head. The siege breaks.

Falling back, Guan Yu finds his own province behind him and his soldiers' families being treated kindly in it. The army dissolves on the road, a few hundred at a time, until he reaches Maicheng with a few hundred men.
chapters.history: Historical, including Lü Meng's decision to treat the captured families well, which destroyed Guan Yu's army more thoroughly than any battle.

pins.note: His army dissolves on the road home.
Talks pleasantly, then offers money for his head.
Treats the families well, and wins.
Does not march.
Advises him not to.

chapters.title: Guan Yu Dies at Maicheng; Lü Meng Does Not Long Outlive Him
summary: Guan Yu breaks out of Maicheng with a few dozen riders, is taken in a net of ropes on the road, and is executed with his son. He is about sixty. Sun Quan sends the head to Cao Cao, who understands he is being handed the blame and buries it with the honours due a nobleman.
At the victory banquet Lü Meng rises from his seat, seizes Sun Quan by the collar in Guan Yu's voice, and falls dead.
chapters.history: The death is historical. The possession is not, but Lü Meng did die within months, which was enough for the story to do the rest.

pins.note: Taken in a net of ropes.
Executed with him.
Dies at the victory banquet.
Sends the head to Cao Cao, and the blame with it.
Buries it with honours, and is not fooled.

chapters.title: Hua Tuo Dies in Prison; Cao Cao Dies at Luoyang
summary: Cao Cao's headaches become unbearable and Hua Tuo proposes to open his skull. Cao Cao, who has spent his life expecting to be murdered, concludes this is an assassination and has him beaten to death in prison; the medical writings Hua Tuo leaves to his jailer are burned by the jailer's wife.
Cao Cao dies at sixty-six, having divided his perfumes among his women and given instructions about his shoes. He never took the imperial title.
chapters.history: Historical, including Hua Tuo's death and the perfumes. The will's preoccupation with small domestic matters is real and has puzzled readers for eighteen centuries.

pins.note: Beaten to death for proposing surgery.
Dies at sixty-six, dividing his perfumes.
Inherits everything but the title.
Has one year left.

chapters.title: Seven Paces; Liu Feng Is Executed
summary: Cao Pi, suspicious of the brother everyone thought should have been heir, orders Cao Zhi to compose a poem in the time it takes to walk seven paces or die. Cao Zhi walks, and produces the beanstalk burning under the pot of beans: 'we grew from the same root — why so eager to burn each other?' Cao Pi lets him live, diminished.
In Shu, Liu Feng is executed for not marching to Maicheng, and Meng Da, who advised him, goes over to Wei.
chapters.history: The seven-pace poem is one of the most famous in the language, though its attachment to this scene is later legend. Liu Feng's execution is historical.
