pins.note: Seven paces, and the beanstalk under the pot.
Lets his brother live, diminished.
Executed for not marching.
Changes sides.
Grieving, and beginning to plan a war.

chapters.title: Cao Pi Deposes the Emperor; Liu Bei Takes the Throne
summary: Emperor Xian, having been a hostage since he was nine, is made to abdicate in favour of Cao Pi with a ceremony of three refusals and three requests. Four hundred years of Han end on a raised platform in front of an audience that has been told what to shout.

In Chengdu the news arrives as a report that the Emperor has been murdered. Liu Bei goes into mourning, refuses the throne twice, and takes it on the third asking as Emperor of Han — the dynasty continuing, in his account, without interruption.
chapters.history: Historical. Emperor Xian was not in fact killed; he lived out a comfortable retirement and outlived Liu Bei by more than a decade, which nobody in Chengdu bothered to check.

pins.note: Founds Wei, and ends four centuries of Han.
Abdicates, and is widely reported dead.
Takes the throne on the third asking.
Who did the asking.
Waiting to see.
Wants the war now.

chapters.title: Zhang Fei Is Murdered in His Tent; the Emperor Marches East
summary: Ordered to produce white mourning banners for the whole army in three days, Zhang Fei flogs the two officers who tell him it cannot be done. They cut his throat that night and carry his head to Wu.

Liu Bei, who has now lost both brothers to the same enemy, refuses every argument against the war — including Zhao Yun's, that the enemy is Cao Pi and always was — and marches east with the whole strength of Shu.
chapters.history: Historical, including the manner of Zhang Fei's death: he had a long record of beating officers he then kept close to him, and had been warned about it.

pins.note: Murdered by his own officers.
Will not be argued out of the war.
Argues that the enemy is Cao Pi, and is overruled.
Left behind to hold the province.
Sues for peace, and is refused.

chapters.title: Sun Quan Submits to Wei to Buy a Free Hand
summary: Sun Quan, facing the whole of Shu with Wei at his back, accepts a Wei title and calls himself a subject — a humiliation he takes without visible difficulty, because it costs nothing and buys him one front instead of two.
Liu Bei comes down the gorges taking city after city. For a season it looks as though grief is a workable strategy.
chapters.history: Historical. Sun Quan's willingness to be seen to submit whenever it was useful is one of the more consistent things about him.

pins.note: Calls himself a subject of Wei, and buys a free hand.
Accepts the submission, and does nothing with it.
Comes down the gorges taking everything.

chapters.title: Liu Bei Wins Everything; Wu Appoints a Scholar to Command
summary: Shu's advance does not stop. Gan Ning is killed by a Nanman arrow; the two officers who murdered Zhang Fei are handed over and cut to pieces at his altar.

With his best commanders dead or beaten, Sun Quan gives the whole army to Lu Xun — thirty-nine, a civil official, with no field command to his name. The veterans refuse to obey him until he produces Sun Quan's sword and offers to use it.
chapters.history: Historical, and the appointment was as unpopular as the novel says.

pins.note: Winning everything, and extending.
Killed by a Nanman arrow.
Given an army that does not want him.

chapters.title: Lu Xun Burns Seven Hundred Li of Camps; the Stone Maze Holds
summary: Lu Xun does nothing for eight months, until the summer heat drives Liu Bei's army off the water and into the shade of the forests in forty linked camps along seven hundred li of gorge. Then he attacks with fire on a night of high wind.

The army of Shu is destroyed in a night. Liu Bei escapes to Baidi with a handful of men; the pursuit is stopped by a heap of stones on a riverbank that Zhuge Liang had laid out years earlier, which Lu Xun rides into and cannot ride out of.
chapters.history: The battle is historical and is the third of the three great fire-battles that decide the period. The stone maze is the novel's — the histories mention only piled stones, and readers did the rest.

pins.note: Waits eight months, then burns seven hundred li in one night.
Escapes with a handful of men.
Whose stones stop the pursuit.

chapters.title: Liu Bei Entrusts His Son at Baidi; Five Armies Are Turned Back
summary: Dying at Baidi, Liu Bei says the thing that has been argued about ever since: if his son is worth supporting, support him — and if he is not, take the throne yourself. Zhuge Liang puts his head on the floor and weeps until it bleeds.

Cao Pi sends five armies at once against a leaderless Shu. Zhuge Liang, who has not left his residence in days and is found feeding fish in his garden, has already turned four of them back without a battle.
chapters.history: The deathbed offer is in the histories, word for word. Whether it was sincere or the most elegant loyalty test ever devised is the oldest argument in the field.

pins.note: 'If he is not worth it, take the throne yourself.'
Weeps until his forehead bleeds.
Seventeen, and emperor.
Sends five armies, and gets none of them home.
Holds the western road by existing.

chapters.title: Deng Zhi Faces the Cauldron; Xu Sheng Burns a Fleet with Painted Walls
summary: Deng Zhi goes to Wu to propose that the two states who have just spent a year destroying each other should ally again. Sun Quan has a cauldron of oil heated to receive him; Deng Zhi walks up to it and laughs, and the alliance is remade and holds for forty years.

Cao Pi comes down to the river in person and finds the far bank fortified for hundreds of li — walls, battlements, spears. They are made of reed matting and paint, put up in one night, and by the time he works it out Xu Sheng's fireships are among his fleet.
chapters.history: The alliance is historical and was the single most consequential diplomatic act of the period. The painted walls are the novel's.

pins.note: Laughs at a cauldron of boiling oil, and remakes the alliance.
Who had the oil heated.
Fortifies a riverbank with reed matting and paint.
Turned back by scenery.

chapters.title: The Southern Campaign Begins; Meng Huo Is Captured the First Time
summary: With the northern border quiet, Zhuge Liang goes south to settle the tribes for good. Ma Su gives him the strategy in one line: attack the hearts, not the walls — a rebellion put down by force will simply happen again when the army leaves.
Meng Huo is captured in the first engagement, refuses to submit on the grounds that he was tricked rather than beaten, and is untied and sent home.
chapters.history: The campaign is historical and the seven captures are recorded, if briefly. 'Attack the heart' is the strategy the sources credit, and it worked: the south stayed quiet.

pins.note: Goes south to settle it permanently.
Captured, and released, for the first of seven times.
'Attack the hearts, not the walls.'

chapters.title: Crossing the Lu; the Second and Third Captures
summary: The army crosses the Lu river at night, because by day the water is hot enough and foul enough to kill men who drink it. Meng Huo is betrayed by his own officers and delivered up a second time, and objects that being handed over by traitors is not the same as being beaten; he is released again.
His brother tries a false surrender with two hundred armed men. Zhuge Liang serves them drugged wine and Meng Huo is carried in asleep, for the third time.
chapters.history: The river crossing is historical and the conditions were genuinely lethal; the campaign lost more men to disease than to fighting.

pins.note: Crosses at night, because the water kills by day.
Taken a second and a third time, and released twice.

chapters.title: The Dumb Spring; the Fourth and Fifth Captures
summary: Pursuing deeper, the army drinks from a silent green spring and is struck mute and dying. A hermit — Meng Huo's own elder brother, living apart from all of it — shows them the herb and the sweet well that cure it.
Meng Huo is taken twice more, once through his own uncle's treachery and once by walking into an ambush he had been told about, and is released both times, growing steadily angrier.
chapters.history: The poisoned springs are folklore built on something real: the southern campaign's worst enemy was the water.

pins.note: Poisoned by a spring, and cured by a hermit.
Fourth and fifth captures; angrier each time.
Takes two Shu officers prisoner, and trades them for her husband.

chapters.title: The Rattan Armour Burns; Meng Huo Submits
summary: Meng Huo's last allies wear armour of rattan soaked in oil, which turns blades and floats men across rivers. Zhuge Liang draws thirty thousand of them into a dry valley and fires both ends, and the armour that would not take a sword burns like kindling.

Watching it, he says he has done a thing that will shorten his life. Meng Huo, taken a seventh time, finally kneels — and the south is governed thereafter by its own people, with no garrison left behind.
chapters.history: The seven captures and releases are in the sources, and so is the decision to leave no occupying force. It held: there was no second southern rebellion in Zhuge Liang's lifetime.

pins.note: Burns thirty thousand men, and says it will cost him years.
Kneels at the seventh asking.
The bait, for fifteen consecutive retreats.

chapters.title: The Sacrifice at the Lu; the Memorial on Setting Out
summary: Coming home, the army cannot cross the Lu for the storm raised by the unburied dead. Told that the river wants forty-nine heads, Zhuge Liang has flour cakes stuffed with meat moulded into the shape of heads and thrown in instead, and the water goes down.

Then he submits the memorial: an account of a mat-weaver who called on him three times, an instruction to his lord's son about which ministers to trust, and a statement of intent. It is the most famous prose document in the language, and it ends with him unable to see the page for tears.
chapters.history: The memorial is real and survives entire. The novel quotes it at length and does not need to improve it.

pins.note: Submits the memorial, and marches north.
Told, in writing, which of his ministers to trust.
Over seventy, and refuses to be left behind.
Emperor of Wei.

chapters.title: Zhao Yun Kills Five Generals in One Morning; Three Commanderies Revolt
summary: Zhao Yun, refused a command on grounds of age, takes the vanguard anyway and kills five Wei officers in a single engagement — one of them a father, then his son, then his three brothers, in order, as they come at him one after another.
Three commanderies west of Chang'an go over to Shu without a fight. For a few weeks the northern expedition looks unstoppable.
chapters.history: Zhao Yun's last campaign is historical, and so is the revolt of the three commanderies. The five kills in a morning are the novel enjoying itself.

pins.note: Five officers in one morning, at over seventy.
Proposes the Ziwu valley raid, and is refused.
Losing commanderies weekly.

chapters.title: Jiang Wei Outthinks the Sleeping Dragon; Wang Lang Dies of an Argument
summary: At Tianshui a young Wei officer anticipates Zhuge Liang's feint and beats it — the first time in the book anyone has. Zhuge Liang takes the city by a forgery specifically to acquire him, and Jiang Wei comes over.

Then the seventy-six-year-old Wang Lang rides out to persuade Shu's army to surrender by force of rhetoric, and is answered so comprehensively — his whole career recited back to him as a list of accommodations — that he falls off his horse dead.
chapters.history: Jiang Wei's defection is historical. Wang Lang died in his bed, two years later, of nothing in particular.

pins.note: Anticipates Zhuge Liang, and is recruited for it.
Acquires an heir by forgery.
Rides out to win by argument, and dies of losing.

chapters.title: The Qiang Are Broken in the Snow; Sima Yi Is Recalled
summary: Wei hires the Qiang and their armoured chariots. Zhuge Liang lets them chase him into a snowfield seeded with pits under the drifts, and the iron carts go in.

Wei's answer is to recall Sima Yi, whom Cao Rui has dismissed on suspicion of ambition. Hearing of the appointment, Zhuge Liang says the only thing that has ever worried him has just been given an army.
chapters.history: Sima Yi's dismissal and recall are historical; so is the assessment that he was the only Wei commander Zhuge Liang treated as a genuine problem.

pins.note: Buries chariots in a snowfield.
Recalled from disgrace, and given the west.
Who had dismissed him for ambition.
Plots to return to Shu, and is far too slow about it.

chapters.title: Ma Su Loses Jieting; the Empty City
summary: Ma Su is given the one position the whole expedition depends on, with written orders to camp astride the road and hold the water. He camps on a hill instead, because the classics say to take the high ground. Sima Yi surrounds the hill, cuts the water, and waits.

With his supply line gone and the army scattered, Zhuge Liang is caught at Xicheng with a few clerks and no soldiers. He opens all four gates, sets two men to sweep the road, and sits on the wall playing the zither. Sima Yi comes up, listens, and withdraws his entire army.
chapters.history: Jieting is historical and was the disaster the novel says. The empty city is a later legend attached to the wrong campaign — and it works as fiction because Sima Yi's caution was real.

pins.note: Camps on a hill, and loses the campaign.
Cuts the water, and waits.
Listens to a man playing the zither, and withdraws.
Opens all four gates.

chapters.title: Ma Su Is Executed; Zhou Fang Cuts Off His Hair
summary: Zhuge Liang executes Ma Su, who was his closest friend's brother and the best young mind in Shu, and weeps doing it — then demotes himself three ranks for having appointed him against advice.

In the east, Zhou Fang of Wu offers to defect and cuts off his own hair in front of Wei's envoys to prove his sincerity, which for a man of his time is very nearly self-mutilation. Cao Xiu believes him and marches into Shiting with a hundred thousand men.
chapters.history: Both historical, including the haircut and Zhuge Liang's self-demotion.

pins.note: Executed by the man who taught him.
Demotes himself three ranks.
Believes a man who cut off his own hair.
Waiting at Shiting.

chapters.title: The Second Memorial; Chencang Will Not Fall
summary: Zhuge Liang goes north again, and the whole expedition breaks on one small fortress. Chencang is held by a single stubborn officer with a thousand men who has prepared for exactly this, and every method Shu tries — ladders, towers, tunnels, fire — is answered within the hour.
Twenty days later the grain runs out and the army goes home. It is the pattern of every remaining campaign: Shu can beat any Wei army in the field and cannot feed itself long enough to matter.
chapters.history: Historical. The logistics are the real story of the northern expeditions, and the novel is honest about it even while celebrating the stratagems.

pins.note: Broken by one fortress and a supply line.
Advises simply waiting.

chapters.title: Wang Shuang Rides into an Ambush; Cao Xiu Dies of Chagrin
summary: Withdrawing, Zhuge Liang leaves Wei Yan behind a ridge, and the pursuing Wang Shuang is killed at a run without ever seeing who did it.

In the east, Cao Xiu's hundred thousand walk into Lu Xun at Shiting and are cut apart. Cao Xiu gets home and dies within weeks — of a boil on his back, the histories say, and of humiliation, the novel says.
chapters.history: Both historical, including the cause of death and its widely assumed real cause.

pins.note: Killed at a run.
Beaten at Shiting, and dead of it within weeks.

chapters.title: The Third Expedition; Sima Yi Loses a Field Battle and Stops Fighting Them
summary: Zhuge Liang takes two commanderies and beats Sima Yi in the open field, comprehensively, in front of his own army.
Sima Yi draws the correct conclusion and never fights him in the open again. From here on Wei's strategy in the west is a wall, a ditch, and a calendar.
chapters.history: Historical. Sima Yi's refusal to engage was sound and deeply unpopular with his own officers, who accused him of cowardice to his face.

pins.note: Beats Sima Yi in the open, once.
Never does that again.

chapters.title: Cao Zhen Dies of a Letter; a False Decree Calls the Army Home
summary: Zhuge Liang writes Cao Zhen, ill in his tent, a letter of such precise and courteous contempt that he dies reading it.

Then, with Sima Yi beaten back and the road open, the army is recalled by imperial decree — because Liu Shan's favourite eunuch has been paid by Wei to say that Zhuge Liang is planning to take the throne. He comes home, and the campaign is thrown away in the capital rather than the field.
chapters.history: Cao Zhen's death and the recall are both historical; the novel supplies the letter, and the eunuch's bribe is the sort of thing that really did happen repeatedly.

pins.note: Dies reading a courteous letter.
Recalled by a decree that was bought.
Signs what he is handed.

chapters.title: Wooden Oxen Carry the Grain; Zhang He Dies at Mumen
summary: Zhuge Liang's answer to the supply problem is a fleet of wooden transport carts — 'wooden oxen and flowing horses' — that need no fodder and can be immobilised by removing a tongue, so captured ones are useless.
Withdrawing again, he leaves an ambush in the Mumen defile. Zhang He, the last of Cao Cao's great generals and ordered by Sima Yi not to pursue, pursues anyway and is shot dead in the road.
chapters.history: The wooden oxen are historical, though what they actually were is still argued about. Zhang He's death at Mumen is historical, and the sources agree he was ordered not to go.

pins.note: Builds transport that eats nothing.
Pursues against orders, and is shot in the road.
Who told him not to.

chapters.title: The Flowing Horses; Sima Yi Will Not Come Out
summary: The last expedition. Zhuge Liang settles his army on the Wei river plain and starts farming it — soldiers and local people working the same fields, so that for the first time the army can feed itself indefinitely.

Sima Yi refuses every provocation. Sent a set of women's clothes and invited to wear them if he will not fight, he puts them on in front of the messenger, asks politely after Zhuge Liang's health and how much he sleeps and eats — and on being told, remarks to his staff that a man who does that much on that little food will not last long.
chapters.history: Historical, dress and all. Sima Yi's deduction from the eating habits is recorded, and he was right.

pins.note: Farms the Wei plain, and cannot be brought to battle.
Wears the dress, and asks how much his enemy eats.
Forbids his commander to fight, at his commander's request.

chapters.title: Fire in Shangfang Valley, and Then Rain
summary: Zhuge Liang builds a supply depot in a gourd-shaped valley, garrisons it visibly with the wooden transports, and lets Sima Yi discover it. Sima Yi comes in with his two sons; the mouth is sealed, the mines are fired, and the whole valley burns.
Then a thunderstorm breaks directly overhead and puts it out, and they ride out through the ash. Zhuge Liang, watching from the ridge: 'Man may plan, but heaven decides.'
chapters.history: Invented. It exists so that the book can say out loud what it has been circling for twenty chapters: that Zhuge Liang is not losing to Sima Yi.

pins.note: Rides into the trap, and rides out through rain.
'Man may plan, but heaven decides.'
Whose torch was late.

chapters.title: The Lamp Goes Out; a Dead Zhuge Frightens a Living Zhongda
summary: Knowing he is dying, Zhuge Liang sets out seven lamps in his tent to petition heaven for twelve more years. On the sixth night Wei Yan bursts in with an alarm and knocks over the principal lamp. He dies at fifty-four, having left written instructions for everything that is to happen next.

The army withdraws in perfect order with his carved likeness seated in the command carriage. Sima Yi, pursuing, sees it, concludes the death was a feint, and runs — which becomes a proverb in his own lifetime.
chapters.history: The death and the orderly withdrawal are historical, and so is the proverb: the sources record it as a joke Sima Yi made about himself.

pins.note: Dies at fifty-four, having written down what happens next.
Knocks over the lamp.
Takes the withdrawal, and the inheritance.
Runs from a wooden statue.
Carrying a sealed order.

chapters.title: Wei Yan Shouts Three Times; Ma Dai Is Standing Behind Him
summary: Wei Yan, passed over, burns the gallery roads and declares against the withdrawal. Confronted, he is invited to do what Zhuge Liang predicted he would do: shout 'who dares kill me?' three times in front of the army. He gets to the third, and Ma Dai — who has been riding beside him for a fortnight under sealed orders — takes his head off.
In Luoyang, Cao Rui builds pleasure gardens and moves bronze statues, and Wei begins to rot from the top.
chapters.history: Wei Yan's death is historical, though it was a succession quarrel rather than a revolt. The silk-bag stratagem is the novel's, and it is Zhuge Liang's last word.

pins.note: 'Who dares kill me?' — three times.
Riding beside him under sealed orders.
Takes over the government.
Builds gardens.

chapters.title: Gongsun Yuan Is Destroyed; Sima Yi Pretends to Be Senile
summary: Sima Yi takes Liaodong in a hundred days and executes the Gongsun family root and branch. Then Cao Rui dies at thirty-five, leaving a child on the throne and two regents who hate each other.

Cao Shuang sidelines Sima Yi, who takes to his bed, spills his porridge down himself in front of Cao Shuang's spy, and mishears every question. The spy reports that the old man will not last the month. Sima Yi waits for the whole family to leave the city on a tomb-sweeping visit, closes the gates behind them, and takes the state in one morning.
chapters.history: Historical in every detail, including the porridge. It is the coup that ends the Cao dynasty in all but name.

pins.note: Destroyed root and branch.
Spills his porridge on purpose, and takes the state.
Leaves the city to sweep the tombs.
A child, and a formality.

chapters.title: Sima Yi Takes the State; Jiang Wei Marches North
summary: Cao Shuang is promised his life and his estates, surrenders his seals, and is executed with three clans a few days later. Wei is now the Sima family's, and everyone knows it.
In Shu, Jiang Wei begins the campaigns he will pursue for the rest of his life — nine of them, against a state with five times his resources, in fulfilment of a promise to a dead man.
chapters.history: Historical. Jiang Wei's campaigns exhausted Shu and are blamed, then and now, for its fall; the novel treats them as loyalty rather than folly, but does not hide the cost.

pins.note: Promised his life, and executed with three clans.
Begins nine campaigns he cannot win.
Sent west to stop him.
Rations his armies to keep the state solvent.

chapters.title: Sun Quan Dies; Ding Feng Attacks in the Snow
summary: Sun Quan dies at seventy-one, having outlived every one of his contemporaries and most of his own sons, and leaves a child heir and a regent, Zhuge Ke, with a high opinion of himself.

Wei attacks across the ice and Ding Feng answers by having his men strip off their armour and helmets and go in through the snow with short blades. Wei's officers are still laughing at them when the camp is overrun.
chapters.history: Historical, including the stripped armour. Sun Quan's long reign and disastrous succession arrangements are the beginning of Wu's end.

pins.note: Dies at seventy-one, having outlived them all.
Regent, and sure of himself.
Attacks through the snow in shirtsleeves.

chapters.title: Sima Shi Deposes an Emperor
summary: Jiang Wei traps Sima Zhao on a mountain with no water and very nearly ends the Sima family; the Qiang cavalry he was relying on change sides at the wrong hour and he loses it.

In Luoyang, Cao Fang plots against Sima Shi with three courtiers, is discovered, and is deposed and sent away — the first time a Wei emperor is removed by his own minister, and the last time anyone is surprised by it.
chapters.history: Historical. The deposition of Cao Fang made explicit what the coup of 249 had already settled.

pins.note: Nearly ends the Sima family, and is betrayed by allies.
Trapped on a waterless mountain.
Deposes an emperor.
Removed and sent away.
Installed in his place.

chapters.title: Wen Yang Rides Through an Army; Sima Shi Dies of a Tumour
summary: Guanqiu Jian revolts at Shouchun. His young officer Wen Yang rides alone into Sima Shi's camp by night, kills his way through, comes out, and then turns and does it again — and Sima Shi, who has recently had a tumour cut from behind his eye, bursts the wound in his agitation and dies of it within days.
Sima Zhao inherits everything, and refuses an imperial order to hand the army over.
chapters.history: Historical, eye and all. Wen Yang's ride is one of the best-attested feats of individual arms in the whole period.

pins.note: Rides through an army, twice, in one night.
Bursts the wound behind his eye, and dies of it.
Inherits, and refuses to give the army back.
Sends the order that is refused.

chapters.title: Deng Ai Reads Jiang Wei's Mind
summary: Jiang Wei comes north again and meets, for the first time, a commander who anticipates him move for move. Deng Ai — a stammering farmer's son who rose on competence alone — occupies every position Jiang Wei intends to use, a day before he intends to use it.
From here to the end of the book, the war in the west is these two men.
chapters.history: Historical. Deng Ai's origins and his stammer are recorded, as is the fact that Wei's aristocracy never quite forgave him for either.

pins.note: Meets his match.
A stammering farmer's son who gets there first.
Beginning to fear his turn is coming.

chapters.title: Zhuge Dan Revolts at Shouchun
summary: Zhuge Dan, watching what has happened to everyone else who commanded an army for the Cao family, revolts with Wu's backing and shuts himself in Shouchun. Sima Zhao besieges it for the better part of a year with the child emperor brought along on campaign so nobody can use him.
The city starves and falls. Several hundred of Zhuge Dan's guards refuse to surrender and are executed one at a time, each asked in turn and each declining.
chapters.history: Historical, including the executions. The sources record that they were killed one by one and that not one of them changed his mind.

pins.note: Revolts, and starves.
Brings the emperor on campaign so nobody else can use him.
Changes sides, and survives.
Sent to help, too late.
Attacks in the west while Wei is busy.

chapters.title: Ding Feng Sets a Trap; Deng Ai Sets a Better One
summary: In Wu, Zhuge Ke's arrogance gets him assassinated at a banquet and the regency changes hands again. In the west Jiang Wei and Deng Ai fight a series of engagements that neither can convert into anything, each of them reading the other perfectly and neither able to do much about it.
Shu is running out of grain, officers and patience.
chapters.history: Historical. The later campaigns achieved nothing and cost Shu more than it had.

pins.note: Assassinated at a banquet.
Who arranges it.
Listening to eunuchs.

chapters.title: Cao Mao Drives His Own Chariot at the Usurper
summary: The young emperor Cao Mao, who has said publicly that Sima Zhao's ambition is obvious to every passer-by, gets into a chariot with a few hundred palace servants and goes to kill him personally. He is intercepted in the street and run through by an officer named Cheng Ji, on Jia Chong's order.
Sima Zhao executes Cheng Ji's three clans for it, weeps at the funeral, and installs another child.
chapters.history: Historical, and it is the moment the Wei dynasty ends in fact. 'Sima Zhao's intentions are known to every passer-by' is still a Chinese idiom.

pins.note: Drives his own chariot at the usurper, and is run through in the street.
Weeps, and executes the man who obeyed him.

chapters.title: Jiang Wei Is Recalled and Sent to Farm
summary: The ninth campaign is going well when the recall comes, bought as usual by the eunuch Huang Hao. Jiang Wei comes home to find a plan afoot to replace him, and takes his officers off to Tazhong to grow wheat rather than stay in the capital and be murdered.
This leaves the northern passes held by nobody in particular, which Wei notices immediately.
chapters.history: Historical. Jiang Wei's internal exile left the Shu frontier effectively unmanned in the year Wei chose to invade.

pins.note: Goes off to grow wheat rather than be murdered at court.
Signs the recall.
Notices the passes are empty.
Given an army of a hundred thousand.
Orders the conquest of Shu.

chapters.title: Two Armies Cross the Mountains
summary: Zhong Hui comes down the main road with a hundred thousand men and Deng Ai holds Jiang Wei in the west so he cannot get back. Hanzhong falls in weeks — the outer forts had been reorganised, on Jiang Wei's own advice, into a scheme that depended on a mobile field army that no longer existed.
Jiang Wei extracts himself by a forced march and gets to Jiange in time to shut the gate. Zhong Hui's hundred thousand stop dead in front of it.
chapters.history: Historical, including the failure of the reorganised defences.

pins.note: A hundred thousand men, stopped by one gate.
Gets there first, by a forced march.
Sent to hold him, and does not.

chapters.title: Deng Ai Crosses Yinping; Zhuge Zhan Dies at Mianzhu
summary: With Jiange unassailable, Deng Ai takes twenty thousand men over seven hundred li of trackless mountain that nobody garrisons because nobody believes an army can cross it. Where the cliffs are sheer he wraps himself in felt and rolls down first.
He comes out behind every defence Shu has. Zhuge Liang's son and grandson meet him at Mianzhu with the last field army and are killed there, having refused a marquisate to surrender.
chapters.history: Historical, felt and all. It is one of the most audacious operations in Chinese military history and it ended the war in a fortnight.

pins.note: Rolls down a cliff wrapped in felt, behind every defence Shu has.
Refuses a marquisate, and dies with his son.
Holding a gate that no longer matters.

chapters.title: Liu Shan Surrenders; His Son Kills His Family and Himself
summary: With one defeat and no army, Liu Shan is advised by the court astrologer to surrender and does so — sending his own seals out to Deng Ai with his face uncovered.

His fifth son Liu Chen argues for dying in the ruins of the city, is refused, and goes to his grandfather's shrine, kills his wife and children, and cuts his own throat. Shu ends after forty-three years.
chapters.history: Historical, including Liu Chen. The novel gives him the dignity the surrender denies everyone else.

pins.note: Surrenders with his face uncovered.
Kills his family at his grandfather's shrine, and then himself.
Takes the surrender, and starts behaving like a king.
Ordered by his emperor to lay down his arms.
Watching Deng Ai's conduct with interest.

chapters.title: Jiang Wei's Last Plan; Sima Yan Takes the Throne
summary: Jiang Wei surrenders to Zhong Hui and immediately begins working on him — flattering his ambition, encouraging him to denounce Deng Ai, and steering him towards a revolt that would leave Shu's officers armed and Wei's western army leaderless. Deng Ai is arrested; Zhong Hui declares; and it very nearly works.

The Wei troops mutiny instead. Zhong Hui is killed, Deng Ai is murdered on the road, and Jiang Wei falls with his sword in his hand, having got closer to restoring Shu after its fall than he ever did before it. In Luoyang, Sima Yan deposes the last Cao emperor and founds the Jin dynasty.
Liu Shan, asked at a banquet in Luoyang whether he thinks of Shu, replies that he is having such a good time here that he never thinks of it at all.
chapters.history: All historical, including Liu Shan's answer — which may have been idiocy or may have been the only survival strategy available to him.

pins.note: Nearly restores Shu after its fall, and dies with his sword out.
Declares, and is killed by his own troops.
Arrested on a forgery, and murdered on the road.
Deposes the last Cao emperor and founds Jin.
'I am so happy here that I never think of Shu.'

chapters.title: Du Yu Splits the Bamboo; the Empire Is One Again
summary: Wu lasts another seventeen years under Sun Hao, who boils critics in oil and flays faces, and whose officers desert in numbers.

In 280 Jin comes down the Yangtze in six columns. Wu's great iron chains across the river are melted with fire rafts and its stakes swept aside; Du Yu, urged to wait for winter, answers that the thing is like splitting bamboo — after the first few joints it splits of its own accord. Sun Hao comes out with his coffin. The empire, long divided, is one again — for thirty-six years.
chapters.history: Historical, chains and all. The novel closes on the same line it opened with, and the reader is expected to notice that it is a wheel rather than a conclusion.

pins.note: Boils his critics, and loses his officers.
'After the first few joints it splits of its own accord.'
Rules a united empire, briefly.
Dies comfortably in Luoyang, eight years after Shu.
